Shen Weici, no matter what, had not expected Shen Zhaozhao would slap her in front of so many people. She pressed her hand slowly against her cheek, trembling slightly. Every person in the room — and there were many — not a single one had moved to stop it. They had all watched with amused interest.

Even Shen Yanli, who had only moments ago spoken up, said not a word now. On the contrary, he stepped to one side and positioned himself to block the view from where the Old Madam and the others sat, so they could not see this scene.

Her heart, in this moment, plunged into ice-cold water.

Her collar was still held in Shen Zhaozhao's grip, strands of hair falling loose. She did not look at the onlookers — only at Shen Zhaozhao — without a trace of cowering. Her voice was quiet and clear: "Does Second Sister not know why I lost?"

Shen Zhaozhao sneered and looked around: "Which of you can say — did I win or not?"

"Was she wronged or not?"

No one spoke. Everyone looked at each other.

Shen Zhaozhao pointed to the Third Branch's concubine-born daughter Shen Mingqiu: "Fourth Sister — tell me, how did I win?"

Shen Mingqiu hesitated. This was purely a Second Branch matter, and she had no wish to involve herself. But choosing between Shen Zhaozhao and Shen Weici was not a difficult choice. She smiled: "I only know that Second Sister's skill in Shuanglu is superb — I could never beat her."

The words were ambiguous, but their meaning was unmistakable.

Shen Weici's eyes blinked. She looked at Shen Zhaozhao: "Since Second Sister's skill is so superior, why not invite the Old Madam to bear witness, and let us play one more game? If I lose again, I will accept any punishment Second Sister sees fit to impose."

Shen Zhaozhao's face went cold: "You are not qualified to play another game against me."

Shen Weici smiled faintly: "Is it that Second Sister does not dare play against me? Or is Second Sister afraid of losing?"

Shen Zhaozhao's expression underwent a great change. She raised her hand high and brought it down across the other side of Shen Weici's face. Shen Weici had anticipated it and moved to block — but Shen Zhaozhao's force was too great, and the blow landed squarely regardless.

Yet this was precisely what Shen Weici had intended. She had already received one slap — if she was going to take it, she would make a scene that the Old Madam could see, let the ladies of each branch witness it; and most importantly, she wanted to push her father, to force him to see even one part of her predicament.

Shen Zhaozhao had been baited beyond reason. She called her maidservant to hold Shen Weici's arms and raised her hand to strike again: "You low country girl — how dare you say I cannot beat you at chess."

"Today I will show you what I am capable of, and teach you to keep your tail between your legs from now on."

The commotion Shen Zhaozhao caused was now large enough that the Third Branch lady-of-the-house nearby came over to see. She called out loudly: "What is the matter here? How did it come to a fight among the young ladies?"

Third Lady-in-law Wang's voice was not quiet, and others in the room came over as well — just in time to see a maid holding Shen Weici's arms while Shen Zhaozhao stood across from her, hand raised and swinging down.

Fortunately, Song Zhang beside them reached out and caught her wrist, and the blow did not land.

Looking at Shen Weici's flushed cheeks, it was clear enough what had happened.

The expressions of those from the First and Second Branches varied. Princess Consort Huimin looked at Lady Wen and gave a cold, amused sound: "Tsk, tsk. The daughters raised by the Second Branch truly open one's eyes."

"Bullying a younger concubine-born sister who has no mother — truly a sight to behold."

Lady Wen's expression changed, and she snapped at Shen Zhaozhao: "Zhaozhao, stop this at once!"

Shen Rongshen came forward and took in the scene — Shen Zhaozhao's ferocious expression, every trace of her usual sweet innocence gone, and Shen Weici silent, not making a sound. Though Shen Weici had not said a word, the fingermarks on her flushed cheeks, the plain look about her, and the slightly loosened pins in her hair all showed plainly what she had endured.

On top of that, Shen Zhaozhao had slapped a concubine-born younger sister in front of the whole household — a clear failure of upbringing. He felt his face flush with shame, and immediately spoke sharply: "Outrageous!"

"Release her at once."

chapters.title: Mockery
chapters.content:
At Shen Rongshen's sharp command, the maid who had been holding Shen Weici immediately let go and retreated to stand behind Shen Zhaozhao.

This whole drama had been witnessed by everyone in the veranda annex. Lady Wen's expression was stiff and grim. She told a matron to go and coax Shen Zhaozhao away.

Shen Zhaozhao was reluctant to leave. She shot Shen Weici a venomous glare, then rushed to throw herself into Lady Wen's arms, weeping: "Mother, she lost the game herself. What was wrong with me slapping her twice?"

Shen Zhaozhao was the only legitimate daughter of the Marquis Manor. In ordinary times she was sweet-tongued and in the Old Madam's favor, indulged by both father and mother, and had never been made to suffer in any matter. Even the other girls in the Manor treated her with some degree of flattery, and so in all things she thought only of herself.

Shen Weici was freed by the maid. She saw Shen Zhaozhao throw herself into Lady Wen's arms, bowed her head, and quietly withdrew into a corner.

Still and composed, as if the scene that had just played out had nothing to do with her.

Shen Rongshen looked at Shen Zhaozhao, then heard her words. His expression dark, he reprimanded: "You and Weici are sisters of the same branch. Even if she did lose, what justifies slapping someone? I have clearly been too indulgent of you. Go back to your room at once!"

At this point the Old Madam was helped forward by her matron. She frowned at Shen Yanli: "What exactly happened?"

Shen Yanli glanced subtly at Shen Weici, then turned to the Old Madam: "It was nothing of consequence, really. Third Sister lost at the game, and Zhaozhao thought it was fun and so patted Third Sister's face as a forfeit — she simply misjudged how much force to use."

Shen Weici listened quietly, her expression carrying the faintest trace of irony.

The Old Madam looked at Shen Weici's reddened cheeks — still faintly bearing fingermarks — which could not possibly have come from a single light touch.

Princess Consort Huimin, not waiting for the Old Madam to speak, said coolly: "Those marks are still showing. Who would have thought the Second Young Miss had such strength? A pat was all it took to leave those marks."

She then looked over at Song Zhang: "璋儿, I do not suppose even the feathered guards under your command have fighters this capable?"

Song Zhang's gaze lingered a moment on Shen Weici, his face cold: "There are some, but they are all brutes fit only for rough and dirty work. I simply do not know where Second Young Miss trained such consummate fighting skills."

He snorted: "Losing at a game and then striking someone — on a level with the common street shrews. Or perhaps surpassing them."

Song Zhang's words were cutting, sparing no dignity. Lady Wen's face went from green to pale, and she could not find anything to say in response.

The First Branch, though they seldom involved themselves in the Manor's affairs, had never been afraid of anyone. Even the Old Madam showed a degree of deference to Princess Consort Huimin, let alone that Song Zhang was a trusted intimate of the Emperor. As an Old Madam without any title, her only real authority was her seniority.

Those in the Third Branch hearing Song Zhang's words could not help but burst out suppressing a laugh, all of them smiling meaningfully — the situation was now perfectly clear.

Words from Song Zhang's mouth were invariably the truth.

Someone murmured low: "Nothing more than the Second Branch bullying someone — and she is their own blood. To be so intolerant of one's own kin...  tsk, tsk, tsk..."

One quiet whisper after another drifted through the room. Shen Zhaozhao's face went white, but she dared not confront Song Zhang and buried her head in her mother's arms.

Lady Wen's face was equally unpleasant. Those stares pressing in from all sides made it seem as though she had been privately mistreating Shen Weici all along.

The Old Madam's own expression showed that she found this ridiculous — but she also had no real intention of blaming Shen Zhaozhao, and so she said with a frown: "Let this matter go no further. The young ladies were just playing, a little too rough — nothing more."

She looked at Shen Weici: "Weici, have you anything to say?"

The favoritism in these words was unmistakable. Shen Weici also had no intention of letting this blow up further here. She understood the Old Madam's meaning: she did not want her to pursue it.

She stepped forward, pressed the corner of a cloth handkerchief to the corner of one eye, and said in a husky voice: "Today's matter was truly not Second Sister's fault. I have caused everyone to come over, and for that I owe the Old Madam and all the ladies an apology."

She then turned and curtseyed to Shen Rongshen: "Please do not blame Second Sister, Father. Weici provoked Second Sister's anger while playing chess — it is only right that I should be punished."

"Yet Weici's appearance is currently disheveled, and she has no wish to disturb everyone's enjoyment further. With Father's permission, she will take her leave."

These words, from beginning to end, were proper and gracious — not a single one assigned blame. She stood among them all, quiet and composed, her beauty undeniable — and despite the fingermarks still on her face, her peach-blossom complexion in spring bloom, her misty, smoky eyes — the contrast with Shen Zhaozhao, who had run sobbing to Lady Wen and still refused to accept what had happened, was apparent to everyone who had a scale to weigh it.

By submitting this way — not contending, not grasping — it showed only that the Second Branch had been too partial, that this newly arrived concubine-born daughter had been mistreated behind closed doors, and even dared to strike her in public. One could only imagine what she endured in private.

The First Lord frowned at Shen Rongshen: "Since you've brought her in, raise her properly. You are already being watched by the Censors — do not let them find grounds to censure you again for conduct unbecoming a gentleman."

In a lower voice he continued: "The household also needs managing. A man who lets himself be ruled by his wife will have a disordered household sooner or later."

Shen Rongshen looked at Shen Weici's downcast brow, at the faintly red corners of her eyes, and felt her silent grievance. A faint sense of guilt toward this daughter rose within him.

He replied quietly to his elder brother: "Elder Brother speaks rightly. I understand."

Then he walked to Shen Weici and sighed: "Go back for now. I will have medicine sent over shortly."

Shen Weici nodded, then raised her face to look at her father, blinking back tears: "Father should not trouble himself over this matter further. Weici is not aggrieved."

She lowered her eyes and, with the maids behind her, quietly withdrew from the veranda annex.

Shen Weici always had a way of gently saying a word or two of comfort to Shen Rongshen — as when she had said on her first day that she did not want to make things difficult for him.

Time and again she considered him, this father of hers, not wanting to cause him trouble. Gradually, his sense of debt had transformed into guilt.

If he were to be honest, he felt little genuine care for this daughter. Since her return, he had barely looked in on her — most of his time was still spent with Shen Zhaozhao.

The words "Weici is not aggrieved" still rang in his ears. He looked at Shen Weici's careful, quiet retreating figure and let out a long, heavy sigh.

Shen Zhaozhao, seeing Shen Weici walk out, wiped her tears and turned again to her father aggrievedly: "She said herself it was nothing to do with me. It was only playing around — she has too thin a skin and so left a mark. That is her own business."

"She had already conceded and lost. Why is she allowed to come back now and blame me?"

Song Zhang looked at Shen Zhaozhao with lazy cold eyes: "Oh? Second Young Miss says Third Young Miss lost? Strange — the way I saw it, it was not like that at all. Does Second Young Miss think I looked at it wrong?"

Shen Zhaozhao stared at Song Zhang in bewilderment. She could not understand why Song Zhang — who ordinarily showed no interest in the Manor's affairs, keeping himself always aloof and uninvolved — should today be saying these things on Shen Weici's behalf three times over.

And earlier, he had also caught her wrist.

She moved her lips, wanting to argue back, yet did not dare. Song Zhang was not someone she could afford to provoke — and she feared he might spell out what she had done with the dice, which would only make things worse for her. So she buried herself once more in her mother's embrace and pretended she had not heard.

Song Zhang watched the whole performance with cold eyes, and when the words were already out of his mouth, he thought himself meddlesome.

Yet he could not help recalling the way Shen Weici's eyes had looked in tears just now — wavering and shimmering — which had given him a pause. He had intended to be a mere spectator, but could not stop himself from keeping his gaze on her.

Even treated so harshly, she had not made a sound. That quietness.

And the composed, unruffled way she had held her gaze during the game — that same stillness, undisturbed by waves.

The Old Madam looked at the retreating figure of Shen Weici, then shot Lady Wen a cold glare: "Come with me to my room."

Lady Wen's heart gave a start. She took Shen Zhaozhao with her and followed the Old Madam inside.

chapters.title: The Second Son of the Zhang Family
chapters.content:
Back in her own courtyard, Shen Weici had been holding back an entire morning's worth of things, and Yuedeng could restrain herself no longer.

"Why did Miss leave just then? We were clearly in the right — it was Shen Zhaozhao who was being unreasonable. I think the Second Lord might well have spoken up for Miss."

In the veranda annex earlier, had Miss not gripped her arm and held her back, she would certainly have stepped forward to argue it out on her young mistress's behalf.

Shen Weici sat in a chair and accepted from a maid a cloth dampened with cool water. She tilted her head back against the chair and pressed the cloth to her cheek.

The cool cloth stung faintly against her skin when it first touched, then became only a soft, merciful coolness.

Her gaze drifted upward to the withered, yellow-brown leaves still clinging high above the window, shaking in lonely desolation in the autumn wind.

Her heart had long since gone cold. She had long since stopped hoping that her father would speak for her.

After a moment's absence of mind, she said softly to Yuedeng: "Do you think the reasoning I could give would count as true reasoning in anyone's eyes?"

"Who has any reason to help a concubine-born daughter with no backing whatsoever? Even the Old Madam framed it as girls playing too rough. I could see at that instant that even if I pushed the matter, it would be smoothed over for Shen Zhaozhao's sake. Better that I stepped back on my own — at least those who were paying attention could see what was really happening, and it was also kinder to Father and to the Second Lady."

Shen Weici closed her weary eyes and slowly exhaled. Unable to help herself, she coughed once: "You should have seen that no one there was going to help me. Letting Father feel a little guilt — so that he might sooner get me out of the Manor and married — is all I want. I never intended to stay here long. Coming here was born of necessity, and I only want to keep to myself and cause no trouble."

Yuedeng stared down in silence, watching the loose strands of hair fall across Shen Weici's face and sway gently in the breeze from the window — soft, and strangely calming to the indignation in her heart.

In this moment, her own heart grew quiet alongside Shen Weici's. She crouched down beside her, eyes reddening: "No matter what comes later, I will stay with Miss and not cause her any more trouble."

Shen Weici lowered her eyes to look at Yuedeng and smiled. Her slender, graceful body curved gently forward as she clasped Yuedeng's hands: "You know me well — I have never thought of you as any trouble. I am grateful that you are here with me. It is a comfort knowing I have you."

Yuedeng looked up, and a tear rolled down.

She had been picked up by her young mistress on a snowy day — her young mistress had been only eight years old at the time, and she herself was a year younger. The young mistress had looked after her, had pleaded and begged her own mother to keep her.

She was happy to be a maidservant and stay at her young mistress's side.

At that moment, the curtain shifted at the outer doorway, and a maid came in to announce that the Second Lord had arrived. Shen Weici started slightly. She handed the cloth in her hand to Yuedeng and had not yet stood when a heavy, steady footfall entered the room.

Shen Weici turned, and saw her father walking in with his hands clasped behind his back, a matron following. He was frowning as he took in the interior of her room.

The room was modestly furnished, the furniture slightly worn, and though everything had its proper place, the difference from Shen Zhaozhao's embroidered boudoir was like the difference between heaven and earth.

This was his first time coming here. Since their meeting before, he had never come to see her again. And between the bustle of recent days, he had nearly forgotten this daughter of his.

Shen Rongshen sighed. His gaze settled on Shen Weici, who had risen and come to stand near him. The red mark on her cheek had not fully faded, her eyes still faintly red and moist, the last trace of tears remaining — yet she watched him with careful eyes, maintaining a distance of three steps as if afraid to come closer, her gaze soft and downcast.

He took a small flask of medicine from the matron and set it in Shen Weici's hand, then spoke — as if in comfort: "I know today's matter was your suffering. I will also reprimand Zhaozhao about it afterward — she will not behave this way again."

Shen Weici naturally agreed with a nod, and said sensibly: "I know Second Sister did not mean it. Today it was I who spoiled the mood. Please do not blame Second Sister on my account."

The more Shen Weici spoke this way, the deeper the guilt that settled over Shen Rongshen. He felt he owed this daughter more and more — so much so that even after being wronged, she did not dare say a word of it to him; on the contrary, she carefully tended to his feelings.

Perhaps the best amends he could offer her was truly to find her a good marriage.

He looked down at Shen Weici: "Over these past days I have already looked into a few families for you. In the end, I have settled on the second son of the Zhang family at Zhongyi Earldom."

"The Zhang family's standing in the capital has somewhat diminished today, but the family's ancestors produced a Prime Minister, and the family has long upheld a clean and upright style. Their background is that of refined scholars, and the household is well-off."

"The head of the Zhang family and I have been acquainted for many years, so I know something of their ways. The second son of the Zhang family placed in the jinshi examination in the twenty-sixth year of Zhizhi, and is of admirable bearing. His household has no concubines or kept maids, and there are no tales of romantic entanglements."

"Through his ancestors' merits, and being particularly valued by the Emperor, he is currently an Imperial Diarist of the Zhongshu Sheng, in constant attendance at His Majesty's side. His prospects for the future are excellent."

"Though he has passed the age of twenty-two, over the years matchmakers have come to call, but he did not consider marriage until he was elevated to Imperial Diarist this year. By all measures he is a fitting match for you."

"You are my daughter — even if concubine-born, with the Marquis Manor's standing and your own looks and character, this match would not be difficult to achieve."

"I have already spoken of this matter with Zhang Er's father. But Zhang Er's wish is to meet you in person first, and I agreed."

Shen Rongshen gave a long sigh: "Zhang Er is the candidate I arrived at after careful deliberation. By the standards of the capital, he is counted among the newly risen. Tomorrow I will invite Zhang Er to my study to talk, and at that time I will have someone come and fetch you. You will have a chance to look each other over. Prepare yourself, for I only hope this marriage can be concluded."

He then looked at Shen Weici: "Weici, are you satisfied with this match?"

Shen Weici's heart sank into thought — she had not expected her father to have found her such a good match. She had assumed he would arrange something perfunctory and be done with it. Yet listening carefully to everything, by any measure, the Zhang Er her father described was an admirable young man.

Besides, she felt it would be better to meet him in person first. She could gauge his character herself — if it proved wanting, she would rather be married to someone from a plain household.

She nodded gratefully: "Daughter is satisfied."

Shen Rongshen nodded: "Good, then."

He asked: "Can you write?"

Shen Weici paused briefly, then nodded: "I practiced a little at the ladies' school I attended before."

Shen Rongshen gave a sound of acknowledgement, said a few more things as if about to leave, but paused when he glanced at the bare, sparse courtyard. He spoke low to Shen Weici: "I hear your stepmother had a few sets of clothing made for you. If there is anything else you are lacking, tell me now, and I will have someone arrange it."

Shen Weici looked at the garment on her body. She was about to ask Shen Rongshen to have a proper set made for her, then thought better of it — saying so would amount to criticizing her stepmother, and she did not want her father to think she was making complaints. She shook her head: "Daughter has everything she needs."

Shen Rongshen nodded: "Then I will go. That medicine works well — the marks on your face should be gone by morning."

Shen Weici looked up at Shen Rongshen: "Daughter will see Father out."

Shen Rongshen met Shen Weici's upturned, gentle gaze — warm and soft, lovely beyond the ordinary — and a rare, fatherly smile passed across his face as he allowed her to accompany him to the door.

Once she had returned to the room, Yuedeng was beaming and spinning about the room in delight, then ran over to Shen Weici: "Miss's marriage is finally settled! Once she is wed, she will never have to stay in the Manor again."

A rare smile touched Shen Weici's face as well.

chapters.title: A Good Man
chapters.content:
In truth, Shen Weici herself was aware that her father had put genuine effort into this matter. Even so, she had not yet met the man — and an inexplicable unease had settled in her heart.

She knew she had no one to lean on. Before she came, she had heard that marriages in the capital were always about matching families of equal standing. Yet the decision to make her way here had been deliberate: she understood that her beauty, in a small place like Yuyang, was something she could not protect. As a woman alone with no support, throwing herself on the household here was her best option.

Still, she was aware of her own origins, and she worried that the other party might find her background unsuitable.

Yuedeng, seeing her young mistress sitting and staring into the distance, came to apply medicine to her face and asked gently: "What is Miss thinking about?"

Shen Weici met Yuedeng's eyes. The light from the window fell upon skin that was nearly translucent in its paleness, and her clear, composed gaze held a ripple of something vulnerable: "I am wondering whether Zhang Er will be my good man — and whether he will be put off by my origins."

Yuedeng gave a quick snort, reaching out to smooth the medicine gently over Shen Weici's smooth skin: "What is wrong with Miss's origins? How much more exalted are the people of this Manor? They were simply born into wealth — and their character is none the better for it. All they know is how to bully the weak while groveling to the strong."

"If he dislikes it, then he is not the right one. Miss will find someone even better."

Shen Weici smiled, lifted a hand to tuck a strand of hair behind her ear, and let her fingertip trace past the corner of her eye where a faint shadow of sorrow still lingered.

By evening, Shen Weici was sitting by lamplight, altering a garment. The ones the seamstress had delivered were all a little tight, and she had taken them apart at the seams to resew.

Shen Weici's needlework — learned partly through her mother's influence — was more than passable. It was not as fine as her mother's, but it surpassed what most ordinary women could do. Even Yuedeng could not sew as well as Shen Weici.

Yuedeng held the candle stand up close so the light was nearer, then propped her chin on her hand: "Resewing a whole garment like this will take at least several hours. The stitching is so close, too. When Miss is tired, leave the rest and let me do it."

"Otherwise your eyes will suffer for it."

Shen Weici glanced up at Yuedeng and let her eyes drop back to the garment, a small smile on her lips: "Your needlework is something I taught you — do not go and ruin this good fabric for me."

Yuedeng sputtered a laugh: "Miss is complaining the work is ugly, yet she still wears the socks I make?"

Shen Weici laughed: "No one can see those — ugly is all right there."

Like this they teased back and forth, whiling away the hours with the easy warmth between them.

------

Meanwhile, on a painted pleasure boat moored on the river, Song Zhang sat sprawled in the principal seat in black house-clothes, a dozen or so men — commanders and guards from his personal guard — seated and lounging to either side.

The room was lively: women in revealing clothing moved between the men, raising wine jugs and laughing and teasing, pouring wine into their mouths. In the center, drums and music played, and the willowy, seductive figures of the boat's dancing girls swayed through their performance.

Song Zhang lay back against the daybed, watching the dancer in the middle. When his eyes met the dancer's inviting glance, his gaze was as cold as if it had frozen over.

A female attendant kneeling beside him had bared nearly half her bosom, her eyes soft and languid as she bent low to pour wine into his mouth, her chest nearly brushing his handsome face.

Song Zhang flicked a glance at the woman, drank, and let his eyes return to the main doorway, where his Left Guard Lieutenant Chen Sheng was striding in with a grim face.

Chen Sheng came to stand before Song Zhang, bent in a deferential bow, and spoke: "General — everyone is in position. Xu Er is downstairs carousing with a woman. Is the order truly to apprehend him?"

His expression carried a trace of hesitation: "He is from the Yong'an Marquis household, and his elder sister is in the palace. Arresting him might make trouble."

Song Zhang gave Chen Sheng an unhurried look: "Am I someone who is afraid of making trouble? Take him directly to the detention ward and deal with him properly there."

Chen Sheng bent close and murmured in Song Zhang's ear: "But that man is, after all, the younger brother of Second Young Miss Shen Zhaozhao of the Jian'an Marquis Manor's future husband. If you arrest him, given that relationship, when you go back..."

Chen Sheng left the sentence unfinished. Song Zhang's expression darkened. He narrowed his eyes at Chen Sheng: "And I now have to look at who a man belongs to before I arrest him?"

The words were not spoken loudly, yet the weight behind them was enough to raise sweat on Chen Sheng's back. He answered at once: "Your subordinate will go and arrest him immediately."

Song Zhang watched Chen Sheng retreat with a darkened face, then sat up from the daybed. His tall, imposing figure carried its own air of menace. His sharp brows swept upward and his star-like eyes were glacially cold — those near him, the female attendants, were frightened to the point of not daring to approach with their wine cups.

He cast a glance at the men seated beside him, rose, and walked in long strides toward the outer deck.

Minhe, watching Song Zhang's retreating figure, quickly waved a hand toward the center of the room. The music fell silent. The lively drinking and teasing of moments before all subsided instantly, and the men pushed their women aside and followed in Song Zhang's wake.

On the deck below, the boat had already erupted into commotion. Seven or eight feathered-guard soldiers were holding the disheveled Xu Second Master of the Yong'an Marquis household while those below scrambled to clear a path on either side.

Who would dare block the way of the Feathered Guards.

Xu Er below was in a state of disarray, cursing and swearing — until he caught sight of Song Zhang descending the stairs, and immediately pointed at him with a shout: "Song Zhang, you are taking your arrogance too far!"

"You arrest people as you please in broad daylight like this — see if I do not have my elder sister file a complaint against you!"

Song Zhang's face carried a cold, unhurried smile. He sauntered to stand before Xu Qing and, in a gesture of deliberate humiliation, reached for the sword at his side and tapped the flat of the blade against Xu Qing's pale, smooth cheek: "Oh? Have you perhaps forgotten — the entire fourteen streets of the capital, outside the inner palace, all fall under my jurisdiction. You dared speak against the imperial princes on my grounds. Tell me, what shall I charge you with?"

Xu Qing's face changed color. He had done nothing worse than grumble, aboard the pleasure boat, that the Emperor had grown old and dim-sighted, favoring that aged Lady Zhang while neglecting his own younger and more beautiful elder sister — and saying he feared the old Emperor would name Lady Zhang's Fourth Prince as crown prince.

Nothing more than a complaint — and yet Song Zhang's people had been everywhere.

Whether the matter was treated as grave or minor was entirely up to how Song Zhang chose to present it to the Emperor.

The Emperor was Song Zhang's great-uncle by maternal lineage. Song Zhang had been raised for years under the roof of the Grand Princess and the Emperor, and the degree of imperial favor shown to him went without saying. Otherwise the Emperor would never have entrusted the Left and Right Guards and the Feathered Guards all to him — only those the Emperor held truly close to his heart could be trusted with such power.

To call him the sharpest hound at the Emperor's side was fitting in every way.

He looked at Song Zhang. Every trace of bravado had evaporated. He hurried to close the distance and began to smile and wheedle in a low, placating voice: "General Song, this is all a misunderstanding. I had too much wine and was talking nonsense. Please let me off this once. Another day I will personally invite you to drink, and I will send a few beautiful young girls to your estate to keep — you will certainly be pleased. How about it?"

He edged a little closer: "And besides, Elder Brother and your Second Sister are to be wed in the new year. If I am in trouble, it will damage the goodwill between the two families. Do you not agree, General?"

Song Zhang smiled — then in the next instant went cold, his lips curling in a contemptuous sneer: "Goodwill? The first time someone has ever spoken of goodwill to me. Shall I take you to the Court of Judicial Review and discuss goodwill there?"

Xu Qing's expression changed. He pointed at Song Zhang: "You..."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow, then made a small gesture to the guard at his side, and Xu Qing was promptly dragged away.

Song Zhang dusted his sleeves and the front of his black robe, and the faint irritation in his chest eased somewhat. Who told the man to run straight into him at such a moment, after all.

Minhe at his side asked: "Where does the General return to? The Grand Princess sent someone to say you have not been to see her for many days — she bids you call on her when you have time."

Song Zhang was escorted out by a cluster of feathered guards, mounted his horse, and after a pause, turned back toward the Jian'an Marquis Manor.

The guards standing where they were exchanged glances. The General had never been in the habit of going to the Manor so readily before — in a month he would stay there three or four nights at most, and spend the rest at the Ducal Manor or his own private residence. So why had he been returning there day after day of late?

chapters.title: Watching Her in the Dead of Night
chapters.content:
It was late at night when Song Zhang returned to the Jian'an Marquis Estate. He dismounted and tossed his riding crop to an attendant, then walked forward through the heavy silence of the night.

The servant trailing behind him noticed the direction Song Zhang was heading and could not help but whisper a gentle reminder: "General, that side gate leads to the West Courtyard."

He had assumed Song Zhang had drunk a little too much wine and simply taken a wrong turn, but the man walking ahead suddenly stopped in his tracks. He turned, his gaze cold as ice, then kicked the servant squarely in the knee. The pain dropped the man to the ground instantly.

Song Zhang had followed his grandfather onto the battlefield at the age of eight, distinguished himself in battle at sixteen, and by eighteen had become the Military Protector of the Western Xi'en Prefecture. At twenty-one he was recalled to the capital, appointed General of the Left and Right Guards and the Jinwu Guards — clearly the Emperor intended to groom him as a man kept close at hand.

A man who had trained in martial arts from childhood naturally had a heavy hand. The servant Minhe felt as though his kneecap had been knocked out of joint. Cold sweat broke out all over him; he could not even stand.

Had that kick landed on an ordinary person, his foot would likely have been ruined entirely.

Song Zhang cast a cold look at the man kneeling in the dirt and talking out of turn, then pulled a brocade pouch from inside his robe and flung it down in front of him: "Go back to the Vice-Commander's Inner Residence and have the estate physician set it."

With those words, he paid no further attention to the man on his knees and turned, striding on.

The Rear West Courtyard was an out-of-the-way corner of the estate. Song Zhang walked along a path carpeted with fallen leaves, the moonlight hazy and dim. He gazed at the modest little courtyard where a candle still burned, stepped toward it, and stood at the courtyard gate.

It was well past the third watch of the night. No maidservant stood guard at the gate, yet light filtered through the main room, where the faint silhouette of a figure could be seen before the window.

The graceful figure was easy to identify — the shadow inclined slightly forward, as though mending something.

He looked for a moment, and his mind drifted back to Shen Weici's face that morning as she had concentrated on the chess game, and to the quiet, patient composure she wore.

Then, following that thought further, he recalled the elegance of her figure and the slenderness of her waist.

Song Zhang paused, telling himself he had been deceived by the surface charm of her gentle beauty. There were so many beautiful women in the world — why was it only her he kept thinking of?

He had come tonight simply to see what manner of bewitching creature she truly was. Sometimes he felt that Shen Weici was deliberately drawing his gaze through means he could not quite name.

He turned his eyes away and made to leave, but then a soft, delicate laugh drifted out from within — as though something had pleased her, like a breeze passing through, sending faint ripples across still water.

This was the first time Song Zhang had ever heard Shen Weici laugh. He stilled, his gaze returning to the silhouette at the window. He could almost picture her at that very moment: sitting with embroidery hoop in hand, drawing the needle through cloth stitch by patient stitch.

Song Zhang pressed his thin lips together. She was nothing but a country girl hungry for wealth and comfort — why did she occupy his thoughts so entirely?

He realized, to his own irritation, that he was even concerned about the slap mark on her face, wondering whether it had left her heartbroken.

But even if it had, what did that have to do with him?

He banished those roving thoughts from his mind and turned, walking away with long strides.

Inside the room, Shen Weici was still sewing. This was her only garment whose color was not too gaudy. Tomorrow she was to meet Second Young Master Zhang, and she worried that wearing it as-is might give people the wrong impression, so she was letting it out a little to make it look more modest and dignified.

Yuedeng was already half-asleep, stifling yawns: "Young Miss, the Zhang gentleman isn't coming until tomorrow afternoon — couldn't you finish this in the morning all the same?"

"If you face him tomorrow with two big dark circles under your eyes, you might end up frightening the man."

Shen Weici let out a small laugh: "You have a way with your arguments."

Her hands did not slow. Her voice dropped: "This marriage is very important to me. I don't want anything to go wrong, and I don't want to miss the chance."

"I want to hold on to this opportunity with both hands."

Yuedeng yawned again and settled in lazily to keep her company: "Then I'll stay up with you, miss."

Shen Weici stayed up until nearly midnight before she finally slept. She rose after two hours and made her way to the main room to freshen up.

Yuedeng looked at Shen Weici's face and saw that, apart from a faint wan tinge and a trace of weariness beneath her eyes, she was still lovely to behold.

She handed Shen Weici her medicine to drink, then said: "After yesterday's incident, Second Madam won't make things difficult for you today, will she?"

Shen Weici drank her medicine, rinsed her mouth with tea, then said as she led Yuedeng out: "We'll see when we get there."

She made her way along the long path to the East Courtyard as usual. The day before yesterday, Shen Weici had deliberately lingered a little before setting out, hoping to avoid crossing paths with Song Zhang — yet here he was again today.

She stepped to the side of the path and retreated a few paces, eyes lowered, waiting for him to pass.

Song Zhang glanced at Shen Weici — still not meeting his eyes — and felt an inexplicable flare of irritation rise somewhere in his chest. He kept his face cold and swept past her without pausing for even a moment.

Once Song Zhang was gone, Shen Weici continued on her way. Yuedeng murmured at her side: "I thought for certain he was going to make trouble for you again."

Shen Weici did not reply. She held up her lantern and watched the path.

When she reached Madam Wen's courtyard, she found her father stepping out with a furrowed brow, followed by Madam Wen's voice, sharp with frustration: "Every time there's serious business to discuss, you run away. Song Zhang may not belong to the Marquis household anymore, but his mother certainly does."

"When a kinsman of ours does something like this — isn't that the same as saying they don't even regard our Second Branch? When Zhao-zhao is married into that family, how will she ever lift her head?"

"It's not as if the boy committed some heinous crime. That reckless idler who never even passed the hereditary examinations — why is he being so impossibly rigid about all this?"

Shen Rong-sheng lifted the curtain and heard Madam Wen's voice behind him. He said nothing, let the curtain fall, and when he saw Shen Weici approaching, he leaned in and said quietly: "Your stepmother is in a temper just now. You should go back."

Shen Weici looked at the closed curtain, then at her father's haggard face. She had no desire to stir up trouble here, so she nodded and turned to leave.

But just then the curtain was flung open from within, and Madam Wen stepped out and seized Shen Rong-sheng by the collar: "I'm trying to have a proper conversation with you — all I'm asking is that you go to your elder brother and say a word to the Commandery Princess about this matter. What are you running away for?"

"The Yong'an Marquis Estate sent a message in the middle of the night last night. We can't simply ignore it. If we do, how will Zhao-zhao ever hold her head up when she marries into that family next year?"

Shen Rong-sheng sighed with a long-suffering "Alas": "You woman, what are you rushing for? You're going to make me late for court — are you trying to get me flogged?"

Madam Wen stopped short, and released her grip — though she immediately shot him a fierce glare: "When you come down from court today, you absolutely must go and speak to them. Otherwise I'll go and make a scene at your elder sister-in-law's place."

Shen Rong-sheng heaved another sigh without answering Madam Wen, and hurried off with his attendants.

Madam Wen watched him flee as though for his life, and her gaze fell on Shen Weici standing nearby.

She looked her over — and stopped short.

She had specifically instructed Xiuniang to make the garment a little too small, hoping to make the girl look as flashy and foxy as one of the women from the pleasure quarter.

Her intention was twofold: First, Adviser Zhang had a taste for women, and she wanted the girl to catch his eye and flatter him accordingly. Second, she did not want Shen Weici to leave a particularly good impression on anyone in the household.

But she had not anticipated that even in that garish, peachy-pink color, the shade only made the girl's lips look redder, her teeth whiter, her face like a blossom — and the dress, far from looking tight, sat modestly and prettily on her. Madam Wen seethed inwardly.

But she quickly reasoned it away. Shen Weici looking presentable was actually a good thing. Before long, the Old Madam would arrange for the girl to meet Zhang Tingyu — and for these few days in between, the girl was simply being eased into life at the estate. Looking pretty was fine.

She withdrew her gaze coolly and told the girl to follow her inside.

Shen Weici looked at Madam Wen's retreating back, then pulled her sleeves together and followed.

No sooner had she stepped inside than she found Shen Zhao-zhao already there, watching her with a venomous look.

Shen Weici acted as though she had not seen it, and greeted Madam Wen with a proper bow.

Madam Wen did not offer Shen Weici a seat. She regarded her with a flat, emotionless expression: "Since your father had you brought into this household, has our Second Branch ever treated you poorly?"

Shen Weici stood in the center of the room and shook her head: "Second Madam took me in, had clothes made for me. Second Elder Sister even gifted me a box of jewelry. You have not treated me poorly."

Madam Wen let out a cold laugh: "Then why did you put on that pitiful, aggrieved face in the inner room yesterday? For whom was that performance?"

"Such a trivial little skirmish — are you trying to invite the rest of the household to laugh at the Second Branch?"

chapters.title: Meeting Second Young Master Zhang
chapters.content:
The room was very quiet. Shen Weici had long since prepared herself for the possibility of being called to account like this.

Madam Wen would never consider laying any blame on Shen Zhao-zhao — she would only ever find fault with Shen Weici.

Shen Weici let a flicker of unease show on her face and looked toward Madam Wen: "Does Second Madam feel I should not have left yesterday?"

"If the other branches have misunderstood Second Elder Sister, I can go and explain right now."

Madam Wen's expression turned ugly. She studied Shen Weici's face intently, her gaze cold and probing, as if she intended to see straight through her.

At her side, Shen Zhao-zhao gave a contemptuous snort: "What are you pretending for? I haven't finished settling accounts with you over what happened yesterday."

"You caused my mother to be lectured by Grandmother — what do you think your punishment ought to be?"

Shen Weici looked at Shen Zhao-zhao with an expression of genuine bewilderment: "Second Elder Sister is going to punish me?"

Shen Zhao-zhao gave a cold laugh: "I'll punish you in place of my mother, naturally. Even if Grandmother has formally recognized your status, you're still nothing but a concubine-born daughter — and a poor, shabby one at that. Keeping you in line is the easiest thing in the world for me."

"You've angered my mother. When the time comes, I'll have you matched with a cripple or a blind man — then you'll have plenty to cry about."

Shen Weici paused, then turned to Madam Wen: "Weici does not know in what way she has offended. But if Second Madam wishes to punish me, I have no objection — I accept whatever you decide."

Shen Zhao-zhao let out a cool little laugh: "Heard that I'll marry you off to a cripple and now you're frightened?"

Shen Weici said nothing and kept her gaze on Madam Wen.

Madam Wen's expression remained cool. She glanced at Shen Zhao-zhao: "You hold your tongue. Weici is your Third Younger Sister — she is a young lady of the Marquis household, and we would never arrange such a marriage for her regardless."

She turned back to Shen Weici: "Zhao-zhao has always been straightforward by nature. In the future, when you are out and about, give way to her more often. If another incident like this occurs — if it grows into a fuss and gives the other branches cause to talk about the Second Branch — then I truly will not let it pass."

Shen Weici obediently nodded: "Weici understands her place. She knows she cannot compare to Second Elder Sister, and in the future will keep her distance so as not to cause any friction."

At that, Shen Zhao-zhao shot to her feet and marched up to stand directly in front of Shen Weici, glaring at her: "What do you mean by that? Are you saying I'm being unreasonable and deliberately picking fights with you?"

Shen Weici met Shen Zhao-zhao's eyes calmly: "I would not dare. I simply know my own situation — I know Second Elder Sister would rather not see me. I would never go out of my way to put myself in front of her."

Shen Zhao-zhao gave a light sniff: "Good that you know it."

Once they were outside Madam Wen's courtyard, Yuedeng asked: "How much longer is the young miss going to endure this?"

Shen Weici was quiet for a moment: "My marriage rests in Second Madam's hands. Although Father is now trying to find a match for me, even if one is settled, the matchmakers will still come to Second Madam first. I don't want anything to go wrong."

"If Second Madam were to interfere, she is my nominal stepmother — she truly could arrange any marriage she pleased. She has never wished me well, so what kind of family would she find for me?"

Yuedeng grew immediately worried: "What if Second Madam finds out about the arrangement with Master Zhang and puts her foot down?"

Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng: "It depends on whether Father is willing to stand up for me. Or perhaps even if Second Madam were truly difficult, Father wouldn't be able to help — in which case I'd have no choice but to let word spread."

"Madam Wen would earn herself a reputation for being cruel to her charges. Let's see if she can still make things hard for me after that."

Yuedeng asked again: "But what if Second Madam is determined regardless? I can see that the Second Master is also afraid of her..."

Shen Weici looked down at the hem of her skirt as branches swept past it: "Then I will have to think of another way."

After returning, Shen Weici reclined on the daybed for another short nap.

In the afternoon, it had barely passed the appointed hour when Yuedeng came rushing in from outside, her face bright with excitement: "Young Miss, the Second Master's man is asking you to come to the study!"

Shen Weici's hand paused. She set down her brush and, for once, went to sit before the dressing table and let Yuedeng tidy her appearance.

Shen Weici had always been born beautiful, and even without ornate hairpins she was a charming, alluring sight that was difficult to look away from.

Yuedeng helped her put on the silver earrings she had brought from Yuyang, and smiled: "The young miss is lovely even without any adornment."

Shen Weici smiled in reply and led Yuedeng out.

Following the maidservant to Tingzhu Pavilion, the girl at the gate spotted Shen Weici approaching from a distance and hurried inside to announce her, then came back out and said softly: "Please go in, miss — the Master is waiting inside."

Shen Weici nodded and quietly lifted the curtain to enter.

Incense burned in the study, and she could hear a warm, unhurried voice inside.

She gathered her hands and passed through the inner screen, stepping into the room — and found a young man in dark-green robes standing with his back to her, upright as a stalk of bamboo, in wide-cut garments and a jade hairpin. He was saying with a smile: "I came upon this calligraphy copy quite by chance. I have already worked through it thoroughly — if it is to Minister Shen's liking, I would be happy to give it to you."

Shen Rong-sheng replied: "My invitation today was no more than a passing impulse. Your father and I are old friends, and I have always felt an affinity for you — I simply wanted to spend a little time in conversation with a young man like yourself. Please keep the item."

Hearing this, Shen Weici glanced once more at that upright back, then stepped forward with her eyes lowered and called out softly: "Father."

Shen Rong-sheng smiled warmly at Shen Weici's arrival and beckoned her over: "You've come at a perfect moment. Were you not just saying you wanted to study Master Liang's style? Zhang Er-lang has a fine hand — his calligraphy is of the proper tradition. Come and have a look."

Shen Weici felt the other man's gaze turn toward her. She kept her eyes lowered and walked obediently to her father's side.

Shen Rong-sheng looked at his daughter, then said pleasantly to Zhang Yuanheng: "This is the daughter I only recently brought back into the family."

"Her mother passed away long ago. She took after her mother's constitution — always somewhat delicate — and has been raised on an estate in the countryside. Now that she is about to come of age, I've brought her home at last."

He turned to Shen Weici: "Weici, this is Zhang Er-lang. You may call him Master Zhang."

Shen Weici finally lifted her eyes to take a brief look at Zhang Yuanheng, then lowered them again and greeted him softly: "Master Zhang."

Zhang Yuanheng could not help but let his gaze settle on Shen Weici, who stood at Shen Rong-sheng's side.

She wore a rose-pink skirt, her eyes cast gently downward — yet at the outer corners of those eyes, a delicate hint of allure curled upward, and just above, a single dark beauty mark. Her nose was elegant and straight, her brows painted as though brushed on. Her face was lovely in the way of a melon-seed — round and smooth — yet suffused with a gentle, graceful warmth.

She was like boundless mountains and misty waters, touched by a single streak of pure white moonlight.

Her voice was soft and warm, the kind that easily stirred something in a listener.

He had come today partly because his father was close with Minister Shen, and partly because, at his age, marriage was indeed something to be considered. He had simply been too preoccupied with his official career before, and with no woman in his heart, he had set the matter aside — he had felt no great urgency to start a family.

But when his father brought it up again this time, he thought he might as well come and see. There was no harm in it.

He had not anticipated, however, that after this one meeting he would find himself unable to look away — that the sight of her, head bowed in quiet grace, would make his heart quicken.

chapters.title: Practicing Calligraphy
chapters.content:
The room was very quiet, filled with a gentle fragrance.

Though Zhang Yuanheng had been momentarily dazzled, he was well-mannered and composed, and did not look at her for long. He returned her greeting with a smile: "Miss Shen."

Shen Weici found his voice warm and pleasant — the voice of someone with a very even temper. She lifted her head and met his clear, unclouded eyes. There was none of the lecherous look she had grown accustomed to from men back in Yuyang when they saw her.

Instead, he was candid and courteous. A single plain jade hairpin was all he wore, and it only made him look more refined — a handsome young gentleman one might pass on the road.

She was already favorably impressed.

Shen Rong-sheng said to Shen Weici: "Since you're here, why don't you grind the ink? Let Zhang Er-lang write something for you to study — watch how he does it, and learn from him."

Shen Weici glanced at the paper already spread on the desk, where a line of seven-character verse had been written. The brushwork was neat and practiced, the strokes sharply skilled — identical in spirit to the calligraphy copy beside it. She was quietly impressed.

She had once tried to copy Master Liang's style herself, but perhaps owing to her weak foundation, she could only write small regular script. The moment any flowing quality entered the strokes, no matter how hard she tried, the result fell far short. She genuinely wanted to learn.

She moved to the desk and began grinding the ink with care, all the while aware of Zhang Yuanheng's eyes on her.

Zhang Yuanheng watched those slender, delicate fingers — pale as mutton-fat jade, seemingly all fine bones — and felt an involuntary tenderness.

He had never encountered a woman like her. The capital, being in the north, tended to produce tall, robust women. Though Shen Weici was not short by any standard, she was on the small side compared to the women of the capital — yet that snow-white, porcelain smoothness of her skin was rarely seen.

The ink was ground. Zhang Yuanheng had a mind to show himself to advantage before her, and so he took up the brush and wrote slowly, stroke by stroke — as though making it easier for her to follow.

From the corner of his eye he caught a glimpse of pink-clad fabric, and glancing further, he saw that Shen Weici was indeed watching his brushwork with genuine attention. His palm grew warm, and for once he felt strangely nervous.

Zhang Yuanheng was writing a line from the Jinsi Lu — he had been reading that book recently and wrote a passage at random. It was, as always, fine calligraphy.

Shen Weici watched with full concentration, tracing the strokes in her mind — and then Zhang Yuanheng suddenly held the brush out to her with a smile: "Miss Shen, would you like to try?"

Zhang Yuanheng's smile was too warmly gentle. Shen Weici felt a faint shyness and reached out to take the brush from him, watching as he stepped aside and thoughtfully spread a fresh sheet of paper for her before she could think to decline.

Shen Weici's calligraphy had not been the finest at the village school, but it was strict and neat — extraordinarily tidy. The women's teacher had once told her to write more loosely, but she was always too cautious, too afraid of ruining a character.

The brush still held the warmth of Zhang Yuanheng's hand. Shen Weici, anxious not to embarrass herself, wrote with full concentration.

Shen Rong-sheng glanced over, and though he had been a little worried it might look clumsy, he was pleasantly surprised to find it had something of its own character. While it lacked Zhang Yuanheng's seasoned authority, for a young woman to produce work of this quality was more than admirable.

He looked at his daughter's profile and thought, against his will, of a woman he had long pushed to the back of his mind. She had raised their daughter remarkably well. Even Zhao-zhao could not produce calligraphy as fine as this.

Zhang Yuanheng studied Shen Weici's brushwork and felt his regard for her deepen by several degrees. The style was somewhat different from his own, but they came from the same tradition. Other than a slight tentativeness, there was nothing to fault.

He picked up a fresh brush, dipped it in ink, and went to stand beside Shen Weici to show her how a particular dot should fall: "If you let the brush turn like this, the character comes alive — it becomes something distinct from the regularity of small standard script."

Shen Weici tried to imitate the way he brought the brush down for that dot, studying him with great earnestness.

Shen Rong-sheng watched them from the side, a satisfied smile spreading across his face. The two of them standing at the window looked like a well-matched pair. If this match could be made, it would be his way of making amends to Shen Weici's mother.

At last, as the sky began to darken, Zhang Yuanheng took his leave. Before departing, he placed the calligraphy copy in Shen Weici's hands and said, looking at her gentle face: "When you have time, copy it. If you have any questions, write to me — I will always write back."

Shen Weici looked at the copy in her hands, then back at Zhang Yuanheng: "I cannot accept something from Master Zhang. Please take it back."

Zhang Yuanheng smiled: "A thing like this belongs with whoever needs it most. For it to end up in Third Miss's hands is its good fortune — a fitting use."

Autumn evenings darkened quickly. Zhang Yuanheng stood in the gathering dusk, holding a lantern, his eyes carrying a calm stillness that put those who looked at him at ease — one could only think of a man of deep refinement and quiet elegance.

Shen Rong-sheng smiled beside him: "Since Zhang Er-lang has given it to you, go ahead and accept it."

Shen Weici could not well refuse any longer. She reached out and took the copy, saying softly: "Thank you, Master Zhang."

Zhang Yuanheng looked into Shen Weici's eyes. The lamplight played between them, and in her dark pupils it was like watching fireworks unfold — his heart stirred.

Shen Rong-sheng asked Shen Weici to head back first while he said a few more words to Zhang Yuanheng.

Shen Weici glanced at Zhang Yuanheng, then lowered her eyes and her gaze and left, clutching the calligraphy copy to her chest.

The moment she was gone, Shen Rong-sheng looked at Zhang Yuanheng with a smile. He dispensed with all pleasantries and asked directly: "What do you make of my daughter?"

Zhang Yuanheng could not help but turn to watch the retreating figure of Shen Weici until she disappeared. Even now he could faintly catch the trace of her soft fragrance.

His expression turned serious as he looked at Shen Rong-sheng: "Third Miss Shen is gracious, dignified, and of rare beauty — I would not presume to offer more than that."

Shen Rong-sheng smiled a little: "Weici has suffered some hardships since she was small. She is a good child — one I hold dear."

"If your intentions are sincere, come to propose early, and treat her well in the years to come."

Zhang Yuanheng heard these words, deliberated briefly, and then clasped his hands before Shen Rong-sheng in a respectful bow: "My feelings for Third Miss Shen are genuine. However, I do not yet know her feelings toward me — to send a formal proposal immediately would seem rather presumptuous."

"Furthermore, my mother is currently at a villa on the outskirts of town, tending to my grandmother's illness, and has not yet returned home — she cannot come in person just yet."

"Minister Shen, please allow me a little more time. If Third Miss Shen is willing to marry me, I will come to propose at the latest after the New Year."

Shen Rong-sheng smiled at the young man before him — upright and well-mannered, accomplished in appearance, and destined for a distinguished official career. For the Marquis household, such a match would also be advantageous. That Zhang Yuanheng could be pleased with Shen Weici was the very best possible outcome.

He took Zhang Yuanheng by both arms, treating him as one of his own: "Your father and I are old friends, and I have long known your character — naturally I trust you with my daughter. I would not have specially invited you today otherwise."

"If you are fond of her, I will betroth my daughter to you — and Weici will certainly agree."

Zhang Yuanheng gave another solemn bow: "I will not disappoint you."

Shen Rong-sheng smiled and personally moved to see Zhang Yuanheng out.

But before they had gone more than a few steps, an attendant hurried to Shen Rong-sheng's side and whispered urgently: "Master, the Madam is here."

Shen Rong-sheng's face stiffened. He forgot about seeing Zhang Yuanheng off and let his own attendant escort the guest, while he turned and doubled back hastily.

Zhang Yuanheng had been about to politely decline a personal escort, but seeing Shen Rong-sheng's urgent expression and the faint crease between his brows, he knew it would be unkind to add to his troubles and took his leave with his attendants.

Shen Rong-sheng had barely reached the study door when Madam Wen appeared with a retinue of matrons: "I get back and there's no sign of you anywhere. Your elder brother has returned — go to his quarters and at least put on a show of helping him deal with this matter. Keep up appearances."

chapters.title: Blocked by Song Zhang
chapters.content:
Shen Rong-sheng pinched the bridge of his nose. He gave Madam Wen a look: "Xu'er was never the reliable sort. Song Zhang arresting someone doesn't necessarily mean there's no evidence. This has nothing to do with us — why should we involve ourselves?"

"Even if someone from the Duke's household comes looking for me, I won't see them."

He turned his sleeve to leave — but before he could take a single step, Madam Wen grabbed him by the ear: "No matter what else Xu'er may be, he is still Zhi'an's younger brother. The man wrote asking for help. Are you really going to do nothing? He will be Zhao-zhao's brother-in-law — with that connection in place, how can you ignore it?"

Shen Rong-sheng winced from the pain, but under Madam Wen's pressure he could only sigh and agree: "Fine, fine, I'll go speak to Elder Brother. Whether it does any good or not — don't blame me."

"When Song Zhang sets his mind to something, ordinary people cannot pull him back."

Madam Wen released him and smiled: "Good. Go — then I can send a reply."

Shen Rong-sheng had no choice but to go.

Meanwhile, Shen Weici was making her way back with the calligraphy copy Zhang Yuanheng had given her tucked in her arms. The sky was only just beginning to darken — still light enough to see the path clearly, and the lack of a lantern was no great inconvenience.

Her courtyard in the Rear West Wing was a quiet, out-of-the-way place, adjoining the back garden, and few people passed through. So she slowed her steps a little and took in the scenery of the estate at her leisure.

Yuedeng walked at her side, beaming: "That Master Zhang is truly like jade come to life, young miss. The Second Master found you a wonderful match."

Shen Weici could not help but lower her head and look at the calligraphy copy in her hands. The volume was in excellent condition. Even for a rare surviving edition over a century old, the paper was still nearly as fresh as new — a testament to how dearly its previous owner had prized it.

She thought of the warm, steady look in Zhang Yuanheng's eyes — the only pair of eyes in the capital that had looked at her with genuine goodwill.

Inside her father's study he had also been wonderfully attentive: he had poured tea for her himself, ground ink for her himself. He had been so quietly considerate that Shen Weici had not even anticipated it.

She rubbed the pages softly with her fingertip, and a faint smile appeared at the corner of her lips.

She murmured: "Whether this comes to anything is still uncertain. Don't mention it to anyone outside. We don't want word getting out."

Yuedeng laughed and clapped a hand over her mouth, nodding vigorously: "The young miss can count on me. I promise I won't say a word."

Shen Weici smiled — but in the next instant, the smile froze on her face. She had spotted Song Zhang coming down the path ahead, leading two large black dogs.

This path was the only route back to her courtyard; no other courtyard opened onto it. She had no idea why Song Zhang was passing through here, but her eyes fell on the black dogs standing nearly as tall as a man's waist, and she took a step back.

Song Zhang noticed Shen Weici's smile vanish the moment she saw him, and the memory of the laugh he had heard from her room the night before rose unbidden in his mind.

It had been fine and soft, like a feather tickling him — it had set something stirring in his chest that would not quite settle.

The sky was still dim just now, but he had quite distinctly seen her smile. And yet it had vanished in an instant, replaced by wary eyes that watched him.

He raised an eyebrow, led his dogs over, and came to stand before Shen Weici: "Is Third Miss Shen afraid of me?"

Song Zhang stepped so close that Shen Weici could catch the cool, faintly spiced scent on him — could feel the warmth radiating from his body.

She stepped back and looked up at Song Zhang's face, half-lit in the half-dark: "The young master is imagining things."

Song Zhang let out a scoffing laugh. Looking down, he noticed the volume she was clutching tightly, and then her wary, guarded eyes — an expression he found distinctly unsettling.

His dark gaze came to rest on her face: "If you're not afraid of me, then why step back?"

Song Zhang was very tall. To speak with him, she had to tilt her head back; looking down, she could see no further than his chest.

The constant craning of her neck was tiring, and she had no desire to look at that arrogantly set face, so she said quietly: "Perhaps it is because the young master is standing too close."

Song Zhang looked at the distance between them — still a full pace apart. Where was that close?

He gave a smile that didn't reach his eyes and stepped forward until the toe of his shoe nearly touched hers, bending slightly toward her: "Now this is close. Would Third Miss Shen not agree?"

His hot breath swept across her face. The darkness around them was dense and heavy, and there was no one else nearby. If some passing maidservant caught sight of this scene and word got out, the reputation damaged would be hers.

Over these past few days she had also gathered some information about Song Zhang's position in the household. Although he had come to the estate when his mother, the Commandery Princess Huimin, remarried the First Master, he still bore the surname Song — he was the sole heir of the Song Duke household, the heir apparent of that family, with no real connection to the Marquis household.

The two of them standing this close was genuinely improper.

Her expression tightened, and just as she was about to step back again, she realized that the wolfhound at Song Zhang's side had somehow slipped around behind her without her noticing. Her retreating embroidered shoe came down on its paw, and the dog immediately bared its sharp teeth and lunged toward her as if to bite.

Shen Weici had always been terrified of dogs. She flinched and snatched her foot back, then looked up at Song Zhang's face: "What is it that Young Master Song wants?"

Song Zhang found Shen Weici's expression — no longer the calm, blank composure she usually wore — rather entertaining.

He even thought those eyes, glaring at him, were quite remarkably beautiful.

His gaze was languid and detached. He bent slightly toward her and, in the gathering dimness, studied the smooth paleness of her cheek and let his eyes drift to those cherry-red lips: "What does Third Miss Shen think I want?"

Those lips were truly small — like a single cherry, with a gentle fullness. Though he could not see her clearly in this light, he could have sworn they were the most vivid shade of red.

Shen Weici had not imagined Song Zhang would be so bold. His nose was nearly touching hers.

She could not understand what this man intended. Or perhaps he simply found her easy to push around.

The autumn evening darkened quickly, and the breath so close to her face made her heart flutter with a panicked feeling she could not quite name.

She tightened the fingers gripping the calligraphy copy, pushed down the strange, searing shame that felt like a slow humiliation, and clenched her jaw as she tried to slip past him to one side.

But the dog behind her seemed to understand its master's unspoken wishes — whichever way she moved, it blocked her.

In the dim haze she caught a glimpse of the one who had arranged all of this: he was watching the whole spectacle as if it were a performance staged for his amusement, and she was a puppet in his palm, being observed with idle curiosity.

She bit her teeth together, then suddenly pushed Song Zhang aside with both hands and darted for the gap she had made.

But there came a fierce, sharp bark, and the dog seized the hem of her skirt in its jaws. She was moving too quickly, and the pull brought her crashing to the ground.

Yuedeng rushed forward to help her — but before she could take a single step, a sword appeared across her path. She stumbled back in fright, her face draining white, and turned to see a cold-faced, handsome young man staring at her just as coldly. The icy light in his eyes struck terror into her heart, and she cried out: "What are you trying to do?"

Minhe did not answer her. He only shot her one frigid look, his expression utterly merciless.

Song Zhang stood with his arms folded, watching Shen Weici bracing herself on the ground as she tried to rise, then crouched down before her: "Third Miss Shen had best not make any sudden moves. When you pushed me just now, in its eyes you became prey. If you struggle too hard, it will spring and snap your neck in an instant."

Shen Weici froze, mid-attempt to rise. Her eyes slowly reddened — but the sky had grown dark enough that Song Zhang could not see the weakness on her face.

She blinked, fingertips scraping against the cold stone beneath her until they stung, and asked: "Why is Young Master Song doing this to me?"

chapters.title: How About Giving Me a Smile
chapters.content:
Song Zhang breathed in the fragrance that was barely an inch from him. He had been thinking about this scent for days — his mind had chased it during his daytime patrols of the Imperial Palace, and it had lingered when he lay down to sleep at night.

No other woman carried this scent. Only Shen Weici.

That faint, tenacious fragrance — like wild orchids growing on high mountain ridges, so light and airy it seemed to dissolve when you tried to catch it, yet impossible to forget.

He thought with uncharacteristic care about Shen Weici's question: why was he doing this to her?

He could not arrive at a satisfying answer. He only knew he found her easy to approach — that he kept wanting to close the distance by a step or two, to find some pretext, to catch a glimpse of an expression he had not seen on her face before.

It was like slowly uncovering things about her he had not known — and that brought a kind of satisfaction no other thing could.

As though he were, by degrees, getting her under his control.

Song Zhang thought that sensation felt very good. At least, he had never felt anything quite like it before.

He made a vague sound, as though genuinely giving the question his careful consideration — yet his unrestrained gaze never left Shen Weici. It was a pity the sky had darkened, and though her pale, smooth complexion was still just visible, those eyes of hers, which always drew his own, had been swallowed by the shadows.

He tapped a finger idly on his knee and glanced down at her: "Now that you put it that way — I suppose I have been a little hard on you."

"How about you give me a smile? Then I'll let you go."

Shen Weici was taken aback. In these circumstances, she could not possibly smile. She tried to pull the hem of her skirt free from the dog's teeth, but she could not get it loose no matter what she did.

She did not want to go on tangled up with this man in such a demeaning situation any longer — and she especially did not want to flatter him with a smile, earning her own release by catering to his whims.

Seeing no response from Shen Weici, Song Zhang reached out and directly seized her by the chin, his face pressing in close: "It's too dark for me to see. Smile now — let me look."

He had her chin in his grip. Her body, braced against the ground, tilted toward him. His face was almost level with hers, their breaths mingling. She felt nothing but deep, scalding humiliation, and the wetness she had been holding back in her eyes could be contained no longer — it rolled down her cheek, silent and involuntary.

Song Zhang felt the warm dampness against his fingers and went still. He stared at Shen Weici's eyes — she kept blinking, and through the shadows he could just make out the glimmer of tears at the corners, a faint rose-pink blush, not a sound escaping her. Yet the wetness against his fingertip was steady and unceasing.

He looked down at her parted lips, their faint warmth washing over him, that particular scent drifting out — and something shifted in his chest. His thumb moved, tracing the smooth line of her jaw, and after a long moment he finally released his grip.

He stood and pulled on the leash. The black dog obediently released the hem of her skirt and returned to stand at its master's side.

Song Zhang's lips pressed into a hard line. He glanced at Shen Weici still on the ground, lingered a moment — then looked away and turned, striding off into the dark.

In that fleeting instant, Song Zhang had felt an overwhelming urge to pull Shen Weici into his arms, to smooth away every trace of hurt she carried — and then to apologize to her with real contrition.

Even to coax her back to calm with humble words.

Song Zhang was furious at himself for the absurd impulse that had flashed through his mind. The only thing he could do was leave, before what was left of his self-control gave way entirely.

The sword that had barred Yuedeng's path was withdrawn. She watched the avenging spirit who had stood in front of her finally walk away, then rushed over and knelt at Shen Weici's side, helping her up: "Young miss, are you all right?"

Shen Weici groped along the ground until she found the calligraphy copy and pressed it tightly to herself. She took Yuedeng's hand and forced herself upright.

The cool of deep autumn made the dampness at the corners of her eyes feel colder still. She said nothing and walked home, blinking steadily, fighting to push the last of the glimmer back where it had come from.

Two lanterns at the courtyard gate — their color faded — swayed faintly in the autumn wind with a kind of mournful restlessness. She stood at the gate and stared at them, at a loss.

The lanterns' light fell across Shen Weici's cheeks. Yuedeng turned to look at her, and saw that several strands of Shen Weici's hair had come loose, her skirt was slightly rumpled, and there was dirt on it.

What made Yuedeng's heart ache was the brightness she could see in her young miss's eyes.

She had followed the young miss up mountain ridges in search of medicines and watched her roll down a slope without shedding a single tear.

Her own heart clenched in sympathy, and she was just opening her mouth to speak when she heard the young miss murmur: "I never want to be at the mercy of others again."

Yuedeng ached for her. She linked her arm tightly through Shen Weici's and whispered: "Master Zhang is certainly a good match for the young miss. Once you marry into his family, you'll be the mistress of the house — you'll never be beholden to anyone again."

"Master Zhang will surely be good to you."

Shen Weici looked silently at the ground: "I hope so."

She left the rest of her words unspoken and walked into the courtyard.

The two maidservants guarding the courtyard gate saw that Shen Weici's hair was in disarray and could not help following after her to ask: "What happened to the Third Miss?"

Yuedeng helped Shen Weici inside and said: "The young miss tripped on the way home in the dark. Go quickly and bring some hot water — the young miss's hands are dirty."

The two maidservants agreed and went off.

Inside the inner room, Yuedeng took Shen Weici's hand and looked at it — and found the palm scraped raw in several places. Her heart broke as she hurried to wipe the dirt from those delicate white hands with a handkerchief, and she said, her voice sharp with indignation: "What is wrong with that Second Young Master Song? Why does he keep making trouble for the young miss?"

"Going around every day with that enormous dog — what if it actually bites someone one day?"

"Is there no one in this household who can manage him?"

"And that aide of his is frightening too — looks at you like a demon who's owed money."

Shen Weici looked at her palm quietly: "If there were someone who could manage him in this household, they would not have let him keep that dog in the first place."

Yuedeng paused, then looked at Shen Weici with a puzzled expression: "Why is it that the Commandery Princess Huimin remarried the First Master, but there are no children in the First Branch — only Second Young Master Song? Where would the title go in the end?"

Shen Weici glanced at her: "You do pay attention to these things."

The hot water arrived from outside just then. Yuedeng hurried to dampen a cloth and wiped Shen Weici's hands with it, talking as she worked: "It's not that I'm nosy — it's just what I hear from the other maidservants."

"Some say it will pass to the eldest son of the Third Branch. Others say that although Eldest Young Master Shen has an official rank, he lacks talent, and his maternal family is somewhat modest in standing, while Third Master is an idle man who drinks and wastes his days — the household couldn't rest on his shoulders. Since the Emperor favors Second Young Master Song, perhaps he will allow Song Zhang to inherit the title."

"Though that is a little hard to account for."

"Anyway, the servants say all sorts of things."

Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng: "Where are you hearing all this?"

Yuedeng said: "The servants talk when there's nothing to do. I hear it all when I go to the kitchen for meals — maidservants from every branch are there, and they know everything."

"And apparently Third Master has worn out his health yet still wants to take a concubine, so he went and bought some special medicines. But the medicines were fakes, and instead he ended up with diarrhea all night long. All the maidservants were laughing themselves senseless over it."

Shen Weici said quietly to Yuedeng: "You can listen to all of this — but you must not join in the gossiping. We should keep a low profile in this household as much as possible, so as not to cause any mishaps."

Yuedeng smiled: "You've said this several times already, miss. I remember."
