She cleaned Shen Weici's hands and went for the medicine Shen Rong-sheng had sent over to apply: "Thank goodness the Second Master sent you that salve. It cleared up the mark on your cheek overnight — your hand should heal just as fast."

Shen Weici looked at the raw scrapes on her palm. The white, cool ointment spread across it brought a stinging, burning pain. The skin was red enough to make one wince.

She had always had a high tolerance for pain. Her other hand moved to her knee, still a dull ache beneath her fingers, and she coughed twice: "Winter is nearly here."

Yuedeng, not looking up, replied: "I wonder if the snow is heavy in the capital. The young miss always hated snow."

chapters.title: A Letter from Second Young Master Zhang
chapters.content:
Shen Weici hated the snow because it made people cold — and the cold made the cruelty of human nature impossible to conceal.

Ashamed that her mother had returned to the family home alone with a child, her grandmother had driven them out without a shred of mercy — only to come knocking, her uncle in tow, the moment word reached her that her mother was doing well.

They claimed the best rooms in the house, seized all the silver her father had left her mother, and installed Shen Weici and her mother in a damp western chamber.

The snow was bitterly cold, and there was no charcoal fire. She had pressed herself against the windowsill and stared at the unbroken white outside, listening to the coughing behind her from the bed where her mother lay, wondering how much longer before the snow would finally stop.

One winter passed into the next. One year into another.

Dressed in a single unlined white robe, she sat propped against the bed, frowning as she drank her medicine. Yuedeng's voice murmured in her ear: "That Master Zhang today was truly a gentleman polished to jade — did you hear how he spoke, young miss? Unhurried and steady, with such a pleasant voice. And his eyes never wandered over the young miss the way those other men's do."

"And the way he dressed — none of those gaudy, flashy ornaments. Not even a jade pendant at his waist; just a flute tucked there instead. Clearly a man of refined taste, not the sort to behave rashly. The young miss marrying him would certainly be a life of harmony and mutual respect."

Shen Weici listened to Yuedeng and could not help smiling: "Your mind has already gotten that far ahead."

"But seeing him today — he does seem like a very fine young man."

Yuedeng giggled and covered her mouth: "Does that mean the young miss has fallen for him?"

Shen Weici smiled a little: "Not quite. But he is warm and courteous, proper in every manner — one can see at a glance that he was raised with great care. A gentleman of that kind is rare."

She put the empty bowl into Yuedeng's hands and dabbed at the corner of her mouth with a handkerchief: "But let's not speak of his affairs yet. We'll wait and see what Father says next."

Yuedeng took the bowl and made an affirmative sound, then went to slide a warming stone into the quilts: "Who knows how long this cold will last. I think the days are starting to feel like winter."

"Is the young miss's knee still hurting?"

It was still somewhat painful. When she touched it, everything felt cold, but the warming stone helped a great deal.

Shen Weici lay on her side with her hair unbound, the dark strands falling past her shoulder, leaving a small, smooth length of pale neck exposed.

She looked at Yuedeng and said softly: "You should sleep early too. You didn't rest properly last night keeping me company — get to bed sooner tonight."

Yuedeng hummed in agreement, pulled the bed curtains down around Shen Weici, and slipped out.

On the second afternoon, a young manservant she did not recognize came to the door delivering something. Shen Weici asked which part of the estate he served, and the boy smiled: "I serve at the front gate, miss. This was brought by someone from the Yiyong Earldom — they asked me to deliver it to Third Miss."

Shen Weici heard 'Earldom' and looked at the small box the boy was holding out, with a letter resting on top of it. She took them both, then asked Yuedeng to give the boy a tip and see him out.

She carried the items to the desk and sat down, setting aside the box and taking the letter in hand, leaning back in her chair.

She recognized the handwriting on the envelope — it was Zhang Yuanheng's.

She looked at the seal of the Earl's estate pressed in wax and felt, for a moment, a slight dizziness of disbelief.

With unhurried fingers she opened the letter. A faint smell of ink drifted up. She unfolded the paper to find neat, practiced characters.

She lowered her lashes and read carefully.

Yuedeng came back in from seeing the boy out, and no sooner had she lifted the curtain than she saw the young miss sitting at the window, bathed in the mellow afternoon light — peaceful and soft, the silver hairpin glinting in her dark hair. Yuedeng instinctively lightened her footsteps.

She stood by the desk and quietly poured a cup of tea, then waited until Shen Weici had finished reading before offering it to her and asking: "Young miss, is it a letter from Master Zhang?"

Shen Weici nodded. She held the letter and stared at it for a moment, then folded it neatly and set it on the table, reaching for the teacup in Yuedeng's hand.

Yuedeng glanced at the letter on the table, curious: "What did Master Zhang write?"

Shen Weici lowered her gaze over the rim of the teacup. Steam rose and warmed her face. She narrowed her eyes against it, and when she looked up again, there was a gentle smile on her face.

"Master Zhang says he heard yesterday that my health is delicate, and he noticed me coughing. It concerned him. He has sent a box of Crimson Gauze Pills to strengthen my constitution — he says they invigorate the vital energy, replenish the blood, and are also beneficial for a cough."

Yuedeng exclaimed with delighted surprise: "I never imagined Master Zhang would be so thoughtful — this means he truly has the young miss in his heart."

She reached for the box on the table and held it out: "Young miss, shall we open it and have a look?"

Shen Weici looked at the beautifully carved wooden box and nodded.

Yuedeng eagerly lifted the lid. A light, unusual fragrance drifted out, and she saw that the interior was divided into ten small compartments, each holding a single pill — two layers in all, roughly twenty small pills, each no larger than a fingernail.

Yuedeng held one up to her eye: "This looks like it ought to be extremely precious."

"I've heard that many noble young ladies in the capital take all sorts of fragrant-body pills, beauty-cultivating pills, and the like. Perhaps this supplement will actually do some good."

Shen Weici leaned against the armrest of her daybed: "Set it aside for now."

Yuedeng looked at her, puzzled: "But they're meant to be taken. What's the point of just setting them aside?"

"After all, they are Master Zhang's genuine good intentions. Doesn't this mean he has the young miss in his heart? Isn't that a good thing?"

Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng and smiled softly: "I am, of course, happy to know Master Zhang's intentions."

"But whether this marriage can come to anything, I still don't know. I don't know whether he truly intends to propose. If he has no such intention — if he only sent these things out of a momentary fondness after meeting me just once — I would rather not keep them. I would return them to him later, to leave no room for anyone to speak ill."

"But if he truly has feelings for me and is willing to come and propose, then naturally I would be happy to accept anything he gives."

Yuedeng sat beside Shen Weici and thought for a moment: "The way Master Zhang concerns himself with the young miss's health — surely he must have that intention?"

Shen Weici gazed down at the tea leaves floating in her cup. Her cold fingers clung to the warmth of the celadon cup. She said quietly: "Who can say for certain."

"He is young, accomplished, and in the Emperor's inner circle — his future is limitless. Perhaps he is also looking for a wife who can offer him some advantage in his career."

"If he were to marry me, I could bring him nothing. All I could offer is to free him from worry at home, to manage the household carefully on his behalf. Beyond that, I have nothing more to give."

Yuedeng started: "I don't think Master Zhang seems like that kind of calculating person."

Shen Weici smiled: "Nothing in this world is ever certain. Let's wait and see a little longer."

Yuedeng nodded obediently, closed the lid of the wooden box, put it away in the cabinet, then turned to find the young miss spreading paper on the desk, as though to write.

She hurried over to grind the ink: "What is the young miss going to write?"

Shen Weici looked out the window at the light, which was bright enough to be slightly harsh. The bare flower branches trembled lightly in the wind. She said softly: "He wrote to ask after my health — naturally I must write back to him."

As she spoke she dipped the brush in ink and began. She deliberately used the brushwork technique Zhang Yuanheng had shown her yesterday. She had only learned a fraction of it, but even that showed she had not set his calligraphy copy aside — it was her way of acknowledging his thoughtfulness.

chapters.title: The Emperor Arranges a Marriage for Song Zhang
chapters.content:
The morning after she sent her letter out, Shen Weici had barely returned from Madam Wen's and finished breakfast when the young manservant appeared again to deliver another letter.

Yuedeng gave him the same small tip and, smiling, saw him out.

Shen Weici rinsed her mouth and carried the letter to the inner room. She settled back into her chair and read.

The familiar seal on the envelope brought a small smile to her eyes.

This time the letter was a full two pages longer than the previous one. The opening, as before, asked after her health, the words warm and attentive — yet measured, never overstepping propriety, so that one did not feel the concern was excessive.

After that, he noted where the brushwork in her letter had been slightly off and wrote out several example characters to show her, patiently explaining each one.

At the very end came another word of concern: winter was nearly here, the wind was cold, and he urged her to drink more cinnamon-bark tea to ward off the chill.

The autumn breeze outside drifted across Shen Weici's cheeks, yet she felt a warm current move through her, a small tenderness touching the tip of her heart.

It had been a long time since anyone had cared for her like this.

Yuedeng came back and saw the smile in Shen Weici's eyes. She could not help smiling too: "What's the young miss smiling about?"

Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng: "I didn't expect Master Zhang to write back so quickly."

Yuedeng said: "That just means Master Zhang is thinking of the young miss."

"Does the young miss think of Master Zhang?"

Shen Weici paused, then shook her head slowly: "I'm not sure."

"But receiving his letter — seeing how careful and considerate it is, how warm and proper — it makes me glad."

Yuedeng giggled: "Then that proves the young miss has feelings for him too."

Shen Weici looked down at the letter in her hands. The words, line by line, were before her eyes. She said quietly: "But I don't want to fix all my hope on one person."

"That way my heart won't be left with nothing when it falls."

Yuedeng thought for a moment: "Why not ask the Second Master — does Master Zhang actually intend to marry the young miss or not?"

"The way I see it, Master Zhang writing so frequently and eagerly — he surely wants to marry you."

Shen Weici set down the letter and rose to go to the low table and unpick the stitches on a few more garments. She said quietly: "These past couple of days I've noticed Father has been rather busy. He wasn't even there when I went to pay my respects this morning. We've only just met a few days ago — it wouldn't do for me to go and ask already."

"There's no great rush. We'll discuss it later."

Yuedeng helped her thread the needle: "Will the young miss not write back to Master Zhang then?"

Shen Weici thought it over: "I'll wait two days before writing back. There's no urgency."

Yuedeng nodded: "That's true."

—

Meanwhile, in the Imperial Palace, Song Zhang was accompanying the Emperor through a stroll in the Imperial Gardens. The Emperor looked at Song Zhang, his expression grave: "I hear you've had Xu'er from the Yong'an Marquis household arrested and sent to the Office of Pending Punishment?"

Song Zhang only smiled: "His Majesty is well-informed."

The Emperor let out a sardonic chuckle: "Consort Xu came to me in tears. How could I not know?"

He stopped walking and turned to Song Zhang: "Tell me — Xu'er is nothing but a wastrel second son. Why did you bother arresting him?"

Song Zhang stood before the Emperor and made a proper bow: "With no Crown Prince yet named, Xu'er has been spreading word outside that Your Majesty intends to elevate the Fourth Prince — the son of Noble Consort Zhang — to heir apparent, stirring up suspicion and rivalry among the princes. Would Your Majesty say he deserved to be arrested?"

The Emperor heard this and sighed: "You are not wrong. My continued delay in naming an heir has become a source of instability. I cannot put it off any longer."

He looked at Song Zhang: "Whom do you think I should name as Crown Prince?"

Song Zhang immediately bowed his head: "Your servant exists only to ensure Your Majesty's safety and to assist with matters that trouble you. The question of the Crown Prince is not one Your servant should presume to comment upon."

The Emperor studied Song Zhang for a moment, then smiled: "You're rather formal and reverent before me these days. When you were small, you used to sit on your maternal grandmother's lap and ask to play with my imperial seal."

"I said you could have it if you wanted it. You jumped straight down from your grandmother's arms and said yes, just like that. Every palace maid and eunuch within sight dropped to their knees. Even your grandmother was so frightened she held you down and knelt — but you stood there before me, bold as you please, as if you weren't quite satisfied with how things had turned out."

"You certainly don't have that kind of audacity anymore."

Song Zhang finally raised his head and gave a rueful smile: "I was too young to know better. And Your Majesty indulged me terribly."

The Emperor smiled: "Song Zhang — you know full well that I have always indulged you because I trust you."

"You are the man closest to my side. With you near me, I am at ease."

"Now my sons are all stirring and jostling for position. I need you to keep a close watch on the Fourth Prince and the Second Prince. For the Third Prince, out with the frontier garrison, send men you trust to keep an eye on things."

"A report every seven days — whatever they do, I want to know."

Song Zhang looked pained: "That many people to watch — does Your Majesty think I can manage it all?"

The Emperor gave him a sideways look: "Why else would I give you command of the Left and Right Guards and the Jinwu Guards? So you could breed reliable men — with that many pairs of eyes at your disposal, you still can't keep watch?"

He clapped Song Zhang on the shoulder: "Don't worry — I will reward you generously in due course. The rank of General of the Grand Armies will be yours, and the prestige will suit you well."

"Furthermore, my most beloved daughter, Princess Zhao-rou, I intend to give to you in marriage. Be at ease — I will not shortchange you."

Song Zhang was taken aback. Seeing from the Emperor's expression that this was no idle jest, he looked at him and said: "Your servant is not yet inclined to discuss marriage. There are still pleasures outside that your servant has not fully enjoyed — once married, I fear I would no longer feel free to enjoy them."

The Emperor burst out laughing: "Honest, at least."

"But your maternal grandmother came to me just the other day to speak about your marriage — asking me to select a fine match for you, someone truly outstanding in every regard."

"And the Song Dukedom has only you, a single heir. If you keep putting marriage off, where are your descendants to come from?"

"Old Duke Song is still out there guarding the frontier at his age — I feel sorry for him. Your marriage cannot be delayed any further. I'll give you six months to think it over. If you haven't chosen someone by then, I will make the choice for you."

Song Zhang looked at the Emperor with a suffering expression: "May your servant make the choice himself?"

The Emperor's face turned severe: "Naturally I cannot indulge you that far. The candidate must meet with my approval, your maternal grandmother's approval, and Duke Song's approval first. Family background and character must both be of the first order — only then would she be worthy."

Song Zhang heard this and gave a pained smile: "Those women are always putting on such a performance in front of others. How tedious."

The Emperor blew out his beard in a huff: "Now you're being picky? Can any ordinary woman compare to a family of good standing?"

"Besides, you take a wife and then keep a few favorites on the side if you like — no one expects you to spend your whole life devoted to a single woman."

Song Zhang asked the Emperor quite earnestly: "Even if I marry the Princess, I can still take concubines?"

The Emperor gave him a look: "Just don't go too far. If there's a scene, I'll be the one with the headache."

Song Zhang only smiled.

He accompanied the Emperor back to the Hall of Diligent Governance, and no sooner had he stepped back out than he turned and found Fifth Princess Zhao-rou hiding behind one of the crimson pillars, peeking at him. He raised an eyebrow and moved to go — but the Fifth Princess darted out and blocked his path, holding out her hand: "Song Zhang, I want you to go catch me a bird."

Song Zhang looked down at the Fifth Princess looking up at him, then raised two fingers to his lips and blew a short whistle. In no time at all, a golden eagle landed on his forearm. He held it out toward the Fifth Princess: "Would you like this?"

Princess Zhao-rou was startled backward several steps by the massive, beating wings, then pointed at Song Zhang, trembling with fury: "Song Zhang, you are bullying me!"

Song Zhang gave her a bored look, then turned his back on her without further ceremony and walked away, the golden eagle perched on his arm.

chapters.title: Zhang Yuanheng Again
chapters.content:
The next few days passed peacefully for Shen Weici. During the day she let out and adjusted garments; in the evenings she practiced calligraphy.

When she went to pay her respects to Madam Wen, Madam Wen gave her no particular trouble — said a few words and sent her back. Even Shen Zhao-zhao had not come looking for her.

Shen Weici felt slightly unsettled by the quiet. It was not as though the cold look in Madam Wen's eyes or the contempt in Shen Zhao-zhao's had been feigned when she first came to the estate. This unnatural calm made her vaguely uneasy.

Yuedeng laughed at her: "Young miss, you're thinking too much. The Second Master must have given Second Young Miss a talking-to after the last incident. They certainly don't want the other branches gossiping."

"Besides, you are perfectly polite and never say more than you should when you go. What could she possibly do — grab you and bite you?"

Shen Weici smiled a little and bent her attention back to the needlework in her hand.

That afternoon, Father's personal attendant came with an invitation to visit the study.

Shen Weici knew the way well by now. She tidied her needlework and left with Yuedeng.

Yuedeng crept close and whispered: "Why is the Master asking the young miss to the study again? Could it be news about Master Zhang? Is he coming to propose?"

Shen Weici smiled: "It probably won't be that soon."

When she stepped into the main hall of Tingzhu Pavilion, she found Zhang Yuanheng already there, seated across from her father in conversation. She had barely looked up when Zhang Yuanheng stopped speaking and his gaze turned toward her.

He wore a plain sky-blue round-collar robe, a jade pendant at his waist, and a faint smile in his eyes as he looked at her — warm and gentle as sunlight.

Shen Weici's heart skipped a beat. She lowered her gaze and paid her respects to her father.

Shen Rong-sheng smiled at her entrance: "Come, find a seat — I was just telling Zhang Er-lang about you."

"Zhang Er-lang says your calligraphy has improved. He came today specifically to teach you. Have you thanked him yet?"

Shen Weici had only just settled into a seat across the room when she heard her father's words. She looked up at Zhang Yuanheng and offered a half-bow: "Thank you, Master Zhang."

Zhang Yuanheng could not help his gaze from resting on Shen Weici across the room. She wore a deep-blue robe embroidered with intricate red peonies on a wide-sleeved background — the open sleeves half-concealing her jade fingers, making what was left of them appear even more slender, each one perfectly shaped.

She wore no powder or rouge, in contrast to the somewhat bright dress. Her hair was without ornament, her skin snowwhite, her lips red, her eyes dark as lacquer — like white snow with red plums: coolly vivid.

He felt a little dazed simply looking at her. He thought of the letter she had sent back — her small, neat, measured characters, somehow a little like her nature: quiet and still, yet in a way that put people at ease without making them feel constrained. Something warm stirred in his chest.

He stood and returned the bow: "Third Miss Shen need not thank me — rather, it is I who have been presumptuous in coming. Please do not hold it against me."

Shen Weici smiled: "In fact I was looking for an opportunity to ask for instruction."

That one smile made Zhang Yuanheng stare for a moment. He had thought her a little on the cool side last time — yet now he found himself thinking that her warmth was equally irresistible.

Shen Rong-sheng had always been hoping to bring this match about. Seeing Zhang Yuanheng's reaction, he was now almost certain — and smiled to himself: "Then let's go to the study."

Shen Rong-sheng did not leave. Since the match had not yet been formally agreed upon, it would not do for Zhang Yuanheng and Shen Weici to be left alone together — that could only invite talk.

He settled back in the great armchair, unhurriedly drinking tea and reading, and left Shen Weici and Zhang Yuanheng standing at the desk to write.

Zhang Yuanheng had placed second in the Imperial Examination. His calligraphy was excellent, his poetry and prose even more so. He was regarded as one of the capital's more accomplished young scholars. It was precisely his friendship with Zhang Yuanheng's father that had made him think of this match in the first place.

He had only intended to test the waters — he had not expected this to have any real chance of coming together. Now he was more than pleased.

Meanwhile, Shen Weici's wide sleeve swept across the desk. Zhang Yuanheng leaned over to look at her brushwork and offered a word of guidance here and there, though his hand remained perfectly proper — he never touched her, pointing only to the level of suggestion.

Yet in the places Shen Weici could not see, Zhang Yuanheng could not help stealing glances at her from the corner of his eye — at her soft, graceful profile, the focused and serious expression she wore, and that single bright beauty mark, all of which made him lose himself.

She had none of the exaggerated, deliberate shyness he had seen in other women, nor the forthright ease of still others. She was quietly, evenly warm — not coy, not bold — and it left him in a state he could not quite name, unsettled in the best possible way.

Since those last two days without a letter from her, he had barely been able to eat or sleep — every time he closed his eyes, he saw the curve of her downcast gaze.

And so, the moment his duty shift ended, he had come here.

He had told himself he only wanted to see her once — to steady that restless, ambiguous feeling in his chest.

Or perhaps he wanted to know what she thought of him.

Shen Weici finished a line and waited, but the person beside her had gone quiet for some time. She turned her head — and met Zhang Yuanheng's eyes, fixed on her with a slightly dazed expression. She blinked and asked softly: "Master Zhang, how does what I've written look now?"

Zhang Yuanheng was, for once, briefly flustered. He quickly lowered his gaze to the paper on the desk.

The characters already had a good deal of feeling and ease to them. He had only shown her twice.

He said quietly: "Third Miss Shen is truly gifted. Before long you will be surpassing me."

Shen Weici let out a light laugh: "I have only learned the surface. I am still far behind Master Zhang."

"But practicing an hour every evening has made a difference."

Zhang Yuanheng heard that laugh and could not keep himself from looking at her again. Her eyes shimmered with warmth, her brows curved gently, and his heart gave an involuntary small leap. He found himself smiling too.

He asked quietly: "I didn't hear you cough just now — has your health improved these past few days?"

Shen Weici smiled: "I took your advice and tried boiling cinnamon bark in tea. It seems to have helped."

Zhang Yuanheng said: "I can see your constitution is somewhat delicate. One of these days I'll send along a few restorative prescriptions — my mother takes them as well. Perhaps they may be of some use."

Shen Weici pressed her lips together and smiled: "You should not trouble yourself or go to any expense, Master Zhang. The household has its own prescriptions, and I am not so very unwell."

Zhang Yuanheng paused, then let out a quiet, rueful laugh: "It is only my heartfelt wish."

Shen Weici saw the look on his face and felt a flutter inside her — but in the end she said nothing.

As usual, Zhang Yuanheng took his leave as the sky began to darken. Shen Rong-sheng specifically asked Shen Weici to see him to the gate while he remained behind — giving the two of them a moment to exchange a few words alone.

Shen Weici walked with Zhang Yuanheng to the covered corridor. A silence stretched between them as they made their way to the courtyard gate, where Zhang Yuanheng suddenly stopped. In the cold breeze, he looked at Shen Weici and said quietly: "I came without much notice today. Does Third Miss Shen feel I was too presumptuous?"

Shen Weici shook her head: "That Master Zhang came out of his busy days to teach me calligraphy — how could I think that presumptuous?"

Zhang Yuanheng looked steadily at Shen Weici's eyes and said what was in his heart: "When I hadn't received a reply letter from Third Miss Shen these past two days, I thought perhaps she found me too forward and had grown displeased with me."

"I told myself to hold back — but I was too unsettled inside. I needed to see you once before I could be at ease."

Taking advantage of the dimming sky, Zhang Yuanheng leaned ever so slightly in Shen Weici's direction. His throat moved, and he asked the question that had been tormenting him: "I wonder — what impression do I make on Third Miss Shen?"

chapters.title: Whether Third Miss Shen Is Willing
chapters.content:
Shen Weici had not expected Zhang Yuanheng to ask her something so direct and unguarded.

She was, in truth, pleased with him — a young man of talent, from a respectable and scholarly family, the son of an Earldom, well-mannered and considerate toward her. From the very beginning she had wanted to make a good impression on him.

But if he was serious, he would come to propose. Propriety and the formal match were matters between parents. Why, then, would he ask for her own thoughts?

These words made Shen Weici's regard for Zhang Yuanheng deepen.

She had only met him twice, yet she felt he deserved the name of a truly refined gentleman.

She had seen the slight daze in his eyes when he looked at her — perhaps he truly had some feeling for her.

The dry leaves at her feet stirred faintly with the breeze. She caught the faint smell of ink on him and opened her mouth: "Master Zhang is accomplished in both appearance and manner, warm and courteous — my impression is entirely favorable."

Zhang Yuanheng felt the anxious weight in his chest ease at those words, and he made his promise: "Though you and I have met only twice, I have already made my decision. Once my mother returns from the countryside where she is tending to my grandmother's illness, I will ask her to come and formally propose."

"Is Third Miss Shen willing?"

Shen Weici was briefly startled, then looked up — and found Zhang Yuanheng's gaze entirely serious.

Those eyes did not look as though they were dissembling. She answered him honestly: "My mother is gone. And my mother was no great family daughter — only an ordinary woman. I myself am not a favored daughter of this household; I am concubine-born, and my dowry will not be considerable."

"I am naturally willing to marry Master Zhang. Only I ask that you think it over carefully. If, in the end, Master Zhang decides not to come with a proposal, I will hold no grudge."

Zhang Yuanheng was about to speak when the figure before him stopped him: "Nor need Master Zhang rush to answer me now. Go home and think it through."

As she said this, Shen Weici offered him a half-bow: "For now, let us part here."

She raised her gaze halfway to meet his: "A matter of such importance — please also consult your family first, Master Zhang. If they are reluctant, I ask that you consider everything carefully."

With that, Shen Weici lowered her eyes and turned, walking away with Yuedeng.

Zhang Yuanheng remained where he was, watching Shen Weici's retreating figure — slender and graceful, her dark hair like a river down her back, those peach-blossom eyes that had looked at him leaving his mind a blank.

She had said she was not favored in her father's household. She had asked him to go home and think it through carefully.

It was a slightly cool and distant thing to say. Yet somehow those words made the warmth in Zhang Yuanheng's chest grow more intense.

They only made him want more to guard her and shield her from harm.

He stood there for a long time, until that last glimpse of her figure had faded entirely, before he finally turned to leave.

He had almost reached the gate when he came face to face with Song Zhang, who had just dismounted from his horse. He hurried forward to greet him with a bow: "General Song."

Zhang Yuanheng spent a great deal of time in the Emperor's presence recording events of significance. Song Zhang was also a constant companion at the Emperor's side. Both had grown up in the capital, and they were at least nodding acquaintances.

Song Zhang and Zhang Yuanheng were not particularly close, but they were on civil terms. He dismounted with a slight nod and asked offhandedly: "What brings you here?"

Zhang Yuanheng smiled: "I came to discuss calligraphy with Minister Shen of the Second Branch."

Song Zhang nodded. The Yiyong Earldom and the Marquis household had a degree of acquaintance. He asked nothing further, they exchanged a few pleasantries, and parted ways.

Back in her courtyard, Shen Weici sat down under the lamp and spread her palm open, studying the scabs forming over the scrapes. They were still faintly itchy.

The weather was very cold by now. No charcoal fire burned in the room. She brought her fingers close to the candle flame, borrowing a little of its warmth.

Yuedeng, who could not bear waiting any longer, sat beside Shen Weici and asked: "Master Zhang all but said outright that he's coming to propose — why did the young miss say all that?"

"If a match like Master Zhang were to slip away, where else would the young miss ever find someone like him?"

"What if the Second Master decides not to bother searching carefully again for the young miss?"

Shen Weici rested her fingers against the warmth of the teacup, cradling it as she leaned back against the chair. The warm amber candlelight fell across her face, bringing out the soft curves of her features.

Her amber-colored eyes shone brighter in the lamplight, lashes long and catching the warmth: "If I had said nothing now, and it turned out that Master Zhang had come only because of the Marquis household, what would I have done then? A marriage made in unhappiness breeds resentment over the years — would that make for a good life?"

"I said those things in advance so he would go home and think it through carefully, and also explain things plainly to his family. Otherwise a marriage made on a moment's liking alone — perhaps it might last three or five years — but as time passes, seeing his colleagues' situations in comparison, how could grievances not eventually arise?"

"I don't want to live that kind of life. Even if I were to miss this opportunity — even if I only married a commoner — as long as husband and wife are of one heart, and can face whatever comes together, without all that scheming and calculation, life would still be livable."

"And I would have a place of my own."

Yuedeng pouted: "But who doesn't want to marry into a good family? The noble young ladies of the capital all aim for the highest matches they can get."

"Once you've married in, what does it matter what anyone says? So long as the young miss does nothing wrong and manages her own affairs well, that's all that's needed."

"And when children come in time — even if a husband isn't ideal, at least there's someone to depend on, isn't there?"

Shen Weici leaned back with a small sigh: "Perhaps I'm only hoping for something more reliable and stable."

In the days that followed, Zhang Yuanheng sent no more letters. But winter set in, and the weather turned cold, and a light, drizzling rain began to fall.

In the mid-afternoon, a young maidservant came to say that the Old Madam had decided that now the weather was cold, she would hold a gathering in the Rosy Pavilion in the garden, to roast meat and drink tea. She invited all the young ladies of the household to come and be merry.

The girl's face was all smiles, her eyes bright and excited — it was clear she too wanted to go.

Shen Weici was not one to go out much. Unlike the other courtyard ladies who visited one another and walked together in the garden, she rarely left her rooms except to pay her respects to Madam Wen. But she could see that the maidservant had been cooped up with her and was more than a little restless, so she agreed to go.

She brought Yuedeng and Hexi along, and set out under a green oilpaper umbrella. Raindrops drummed down onto it in a light scatter, splashing into puddles at her feet and lightly wetting the toes of her embroidered shoes.

The garden was vast — Taihu stones and flowering trees layered and interlocked at every turn, a stream threading its way through. The carp inside had retreated to shelter beneath the garden rockery.

Shen Yen-li, seated sideways on the railing, spotted Shen Weici's figure approaching from a distance with her umbrella and turned back to say to Song Zhang, who was sitting at his side: "I didn't expect you'd actually remember that Third Younger Sister wasn't there. Even I forgot."

Song Zhang said nothing. His deep, dark gaze rested on the figure who had just stepped up onto the arching stone bridge — the rain muting the colors of her dress, flickering and indistinct.

Shen Si-wen looked at Song Zhang and, seeing he made no reply, thought better of pressing the matter. But it was odd to him — this was a man who never came to these sorts of gatherings. He had only said a word in passing, and somehow Song Zhang had actually come.

And having come, he had done nothing — neither eaten nor talked — sitting there with that glacial, forbidding air that made Shen Si-wen feel inexplicably inhibited in his own conversation.

He had barely spent time in the estate at all before. Why was he suddenly so at leisure?

Shen Weici meanwhile held her skirt hem with two fingers and picked her way along the path until she finally arrived.

The pavilion had three stories. The Old Madam and the others were on the third floor. A few maidservants guarded the lower floors. Seeing another guest arrive, one of them came forward to take the cloak she had unfastened and carry it to the side room to dry on a rack.

Shen Weici turned and looked at the rippling surface of the green pool behind her, then lowered her gaze and climbed the stairs.

The lively sounds of laughter could already be heard from below; reaching the top, they were louder still. Warmth swept over her, and the joking and chatter rang out one after another.

Shen Weici paused at the top of the stairs. No one seemed to have noticed her. She saw that everyone was gathered around the roasting brazier. The Old Madam sat at the head, surrounded by the unmarried young ladies of the household, talking and laughing. To one side stood Shen Yen-li and the Fourth Young Master Shen Si-wen, both smiling and joining in.

Shen Weici stood at the corner of the stairwell, listening to the sounds of merriment. She suddenly felt like an outsider.

The rack above was already laden with several roasted pieces of meat. Everyone was all present; she was the last to arrive. It was obvious she had been remembered partway through and sent for.

The matron standing at the Old Madam's side spotted Shen Weici and called out warmly: "Third Miss is here — the Old Madam has been asking about you."

That one remark drew all eyes toward her. Shen Zhao-zhao looked at Shen Weici wearing those flashy colors so well and could not suppress a flicker of jealousy, responding with a cold, dismissive sound.

Feeling all those gazes on her, Shen Weici pressed down the thoughts that stirred in her chest, put on a smile, and walked over to pay her respects to the Old Madam.

From the corner of her eye she caught sight of Song Zhang too, and looked away.

Shen Old Madam smiled and patted the space beside her: "Come sit with me, child." Then, to Shen Yen-li: "Your Third Sister is here — pour her a small cup of warm wine to take the chill off."

chapters.title: The Flying Flower Poetry Game
chapters.content:
Shen Weici settled beside the Old Madam. The chill she had carried in from outside was quickly warmed away by the press of people around her.

She looked at the small pink porcelain cup Shen Yen-li was smiling and holding out, and heard him say: "Third Younger Sister, this is cherry wine — there is rose honey in it as well. It is wonderfully sweet and fragrant, and I promise you will want more once you've tasted it."

Shen Weici had never drunk wine before. She was on the verge of declining, but seeing that no one else had said anything, and that Shen Yen-li was already holding the cup right up to her, and that it was the Old Madam who had asked — she could not well refuse and spoil the mood. She took it with a small smile.

She glanced at the cup and took a delicate sip — faintly sour, faintly sweet, with the barest suggestion of wine. Not particularly unpleasant, but not quite pleasant either.

It was her first time drinking, and she took only one sip. Shen Yen-li noticed and immediately made a show of urging her on: "Who drinks wine one sip at a time? Even Fifth Younger Sister can knock back three cups in a row — how can Third Younger Sister not finish at least one cup?"

Shen Zhao-zhao's lip curled coldly: "I'd say she's never had anything good and wouldn't know how to appreciate it if you gave it to her."

The Old Madam said to Shen Weici at her side: "Fruit wine doesn't make you drunk. Drinking it all in one go is the only way to warm yourself up properly."

With the Old Madam saying so, Shen Weici had little choice but to drink the whole cup.

The empty cup was quickly refilled by Shen Yen-li, though to his credit he did not press her further. He and Shen Si-wen busied themselves with slicing and roasting meat.

Once the meat was roasted and salt sprinkled over it, the savory aroma rose around them. Outside, cold rain fell on and on. Inside, they circled the brazier eating meat and drinking wine, watching the rain-drenched view — it was its own kind of pleasure.

Shen Weici was given a pair of silver chopsticks and picked up a small piece to try.

The talk continued and the gathering stayed lively, but Shen Weici could not join in. She took a couple of bites and sat quietly listening.

They spoke mostly of happenings in the capital — which two families had become engaged, what incident had occurred in someone else's household. In the capital, everyone's affairs were intertwined; the great families were mostly acquainted with one another, and even those they didn't know well could supply some interesting piece of gossip.

She was listening quietly to all of it when the Old Madam suddenly took her hand and said: "On ordinary days, go out and chat with people. Don't sit alone in your courtyard — it must be dull, mustn't it?"

"Walk around the garden more, and spend time with the young ladies here — get to know one another better."

Shen Weici nodded with docile compliance: "Please don't worry on my account, Old Madam. I'll remember."

Shen Old Madam studied Shen Weici's face carefully. Among all the young ladies of the household, she was undeniably the most beautiful, and her bearing and conduct were equally fine — gentle and composed, without any of the recklessness or wild swings of mood that youth sometimes brought. A temperament like that was rare.

A faint pang of guilt toward the girl stirred in the Old Madam's heart.

She also noticed that Shen Weici's hair still had not a single ornament — no eardrops, no bracelets — and that she relied on nothing but her face to stand out. She asked: "I see you have no jewelry on you at all. Is it that you haven't any, or you simply don't wear it?"

At those words, Shen Weici felt a sharp look lance toward her from somewhere nearby. Her expression did not change. She looked at the Old Madam and said quietly: "My stepmother arranged a great many pieces of jewelry for me, and Second Elder Sister gave me a whole boxful as well. But I was never in the habit of wearing jewelry, and I worry about losing pieces that are too valuable — I thought I would save them for more important occasions."

Shen Zhao-zhao heard this and gave a thin, contemptuous laugh: "Giving nice things to her really is a waste."

Shen Old Madam frowned at Shen Zhao-zhao: "Hold your tongue. You are sisters — you should get along."

Shen Zhao-zhao, who had never been addressed so sternly by her grandmother, was startled into silence.

Shen Old Madam turned back to Shen Weici: "It won't do to go without jewelry. At the very least you are now a young lady of the Marquis household. If people from outside were to see you, they might think the household has given you nothing."

Shen Weici looked up at the Old Madam: "Then I will do as the Old Madam says."

Shen Old Madam smiled and patted the back of Shen Weici's hand.

Song Zhang seemed equally out of place in the noisy gathering. He stared out at the lake through the pavilion windows. Even when Shen Si-wen and Shen Yen-li came to make conversation, he barely responded. The roasted meat the maidservants brought him sat untouched.

Only his gaze would drift, every now and then, from the window to Shen Weici — sitting at the Old Madam's side with her eyes lowered and a smile at her lips.

Minhe, who stood at Song Zhang's side, could not make sense of his general's mind. At noon Song Zhang had come back to the estate saying he needed to change clothes before heading to the training grounds to drill and select men. Clearly that plan had been abandoned. But why was he sitting here of all places?

The roasted meat was gradually finished. Shen Weici had eaten only a piece or two.

It was the first time she had tried venison — it tasted good, though she was not used to it and found it somehow too gamey. Besides, only a small amount was roasted at once, and she always waited until everyone else had helped themselves first, so there was nothing left by the time it got to her.

The fruit wine, however, she found she liked well enough after a cup or two — the slight bitterness beneath the rich fragrance was somehow pleasing once you got used to it.

Whenever her cup was empty, a maidservant appeared to refill it. Without quite noticing, she had drunk three or four cups.

Outside, the rain grew heavier. It showed no sign of stopping.

The Old Madam had eventually grown tired, and was helped back to her rooms by an attendant matron.

Once the Old Madam was gone, those who remained felt free to talk as they pleased. After the roasted meat was finished, they started up a game of the Flying Flower Poetry Challenge, with 'rain' as the designated character. Anyone who could not produce a matching line would be penalized with wine.

The Flying Flower Challenge was not inherently difficult — one could cite lines from classical poets, or compose something on the spot.

But Shen Zhao-zhao looked at Shen Weici and said they must compose something new on the spot; if you failed, the penalty was three cups.

She even looked pointedly at Shen Weici: "Third Younger Sister, you may not opt out."

Shen Yen-li saw this and said: "Third Younger Sister probably hasn't had much formal schooling. Don't make it hard for her — let's keep the original rules."

He turned to Shen Weici: "Third Younger Sister, don't mind what Zhao-zhao says."

Shen Weici sat beside the brazier. The warmth had brought a faint blush of pink to her fair cheeks, and her fingers, so cold earlier, had gradually thawed.

She heard Shen Yen-li's words and finally raised her eyes from their downward cast. She said lightly: "I will go along with whatever the elder and younger sisters decide. I only ask not to ruin everyone's fun."

Shen Zhao-zhao let out a cold laugh and tugged at her brother's sleeve: "Hear that? She doesn't appreciate your kindness. Why are you going out of your way for her?"

Shen Yen-li blinked and looked again at Shen Weici — at her lightly flushed cheeks, and her eyes lifting toward him, soft and unhurried.

Someone else spoke up: "Let's just go with Second Elder Sister's version — more of a challenge makes it more fun. We're all playing together; what matters is to participate."

Shen Yen-li let the matter drop, and asked a maidservant to bring out the bamboo drawing-sticks. He glanced at Song Zhang beside him, wanting to invite him in, but not quite daring.

Song Zhang looked at Shen Yen-li: "Play without me."

Shen Yen-li relaxed with relief.

Everyone drew a stick. Shen Weici looked at hers — she had drawn last.

Shen Zhao-zhao went first. With only half a sandglass of time to compose a matching couplet on the spot, it was genuinely challenging.

Most people managed by borrowing a line from older poetry and reworking the meter.

After two rounds, when it was Shen Yen-li's turn, he could not think of anything and took his penalty cup himself.

When it came to Shen Weici, she thought briefly and then said: "One night's rain falls without measure, and by morning shows no sign of yielding."

The others stared, surprised. No one had expected Shen Weici to come up with something so quickly.

Shen Zhao-zhao was irritated. She had been praised by the clan's teachers since childhood, and her poetry was considered the best in the household. No one else here could produce something so quickly — not even she could always manage it on the first try.

She quickly thought up her own line, but her eyes stayed fixed on Shen Weici.

In the next round, Fifth Young Miss was too young and naturally could not manage; Fourth Young Miss barely scraped through; Shen Si-wen produced something at the very last moment; Shen Yen-li simply gave up.

Shen Weici looked out at the rainy view and without much thought spoke: "Moss creeps over crumbling walls as autumn deepens; grass swallows broken ramparts, rain swallows more."

This verse carried a desolate, wistful feeling — like a place left by all who mattered, its warmth gone with them.

Every person in the room turned to look at Shen Weici. None of them could quite reconcile what they were seeing — a girl from the countryside who apparently had more feeling for poetry than any of them.

Song Zhang's eyes settled on Shen Weici's face — her cheeks flushed a vivid peach-pink, her inherently alluring face looking, in this moment, as though it might dissolve into the rain.

Those eyes, half-lowered and gleaming with warmth in the sound of the rain, and the line of poetry that came from those cherry-red lips — Song Zhang's gaze was almost unable to look away.

Seeing Shen Weici come through again, Shen Zhao-zhao's composure finally cracked. The sandglass was nearly run out, everyone was watching her — and she only barely produced a line in the final moment.

Shen Weici had already taken note of the look on Shen Zhao-zhao's face. In this round, no one else could answer, and it was Shen Weici's turn.

Yuedeng, seated nearby, was quietly thrilled, waiting for her young miss to shine.

She knew her young miss would certainly find an answer. The young miss had the best ear for rhyme and meter — the teacher at the village school had praised her again and again, saying she had the mind of a scholar who could sit the imperial examinations and earn a degree.

Besides, the young miss had just whispered a line to her ear not long ago: "Rain pounds all night and rushes headlong into dawn; from all four mountains, clouded air presses toward the autumn cold." She had been teaching Yuedeng to recognize the rhyme scheme — it was already composed.

But to Yuedeng's surprise, she watched the young miss furrow her brows as if thinking very hard, her eyes fixed on the sandglass, and not produce a single word until the very last grain had fallen.

chapters.title: Hidden Gems
chapters.content:
Shen Weici scrunched her brows gently, as though deep in genuine thought, her eyes fixed on the sandglass — and at the very last moment said softly: "I can't think of anything. Second Elder Sister is far better than me at this. I'll take my penalty willingly."

With that, Shen Weici took the cup from the maidservant's hand and drank all three cups of warm wine.

Shen Zhao-zhao had been on the verge of failing herself in the next round — and if she, a proper well-bred daughter of the Marquis household, had lost to Shen Weici, the humiliation would have been unbearable.

It was lucky that, even though Shen Weici had surprised her somewhat, it had only come to this.

The smile she wore turned superior. She cast Shen Weici a condescending look: "Third Younger Sister actually held her own for this many rounds — that's not bad at all."

Fourth Young Miss Shen Mingqiu said with a smile: "Even so, Third Elder Sister was impressive — I didn't expect it at all."

Shen Mingqiu genuinely felt a new respect for Shen Weici. The time they had played the dice-board game before — somehow Shen Weici had drawn with Shen Zhao-zhao, which was remarkable in itself, since a draw at dice was rare. She had already found that astonishing.

Shen Weici smiled warmly: "I was only muddling through by luck. I can't really claim credit for it."

"Fourth Younger Sister and Fifth Younger Sister, if they truly applied themselves, would surpass me without difficulty."

Shen Si-wen looked at Shen Weici: "Third Younger Cousin, you really are full of surprises. Did you study before?"

Shen Weici's eyes still held their quiet warmth: "I picked up a few things, but only barely scratched the surface."

"Honestly, I can't compare to Eldest Cousin or any of the sisters here."

As she spoke she rose from her chair and excused herself: "It looks as though the rain isn't going to let up. My courtyard is a little out of the way — I'll head back first."

She had just lifted her foot when Shen Zhao-zhao reached out and caught her: "Third Younger Sister, you've only played one round and you're leaving? Where's the fun in that? Surely Third Younger Sister should stay for at least three rounds."

Shen Zhao-zhao had had no intention of making trouble for Shen Weici. But when Shen Weici had shown herself more capable, and everyone had praised her for it — even the people who hadn't particularly liked her before — Shen Zhao-zhao couldn't stomach it. She had to do something.

Shen Weici paused and looked down at Shen Zhao-zhao seated in her chair — her eyes full of contemptuous disdain, with a flicker of something malicious underneath, as if Shen Weici's discomfiture brought her satisfaction.

Shen Weici had no desire for conflict with Shen Zhao-zhao. They were both of the Second Branch; any clash between them would only hurt her own position.

But perhaps it was the wine working through her now — that fruit wine that seemed so mild was beginning to have its effect, making her body warm and her head faintly light.

She smiled: "The sky looks as though it's nearly dark — if Second Elder Sister wants to play on, how about I come over tomorrow and keep you company?"

Shen Zhao-zhao gave her a look: "It's still quite bright out. Perhaps it'll be over quickly. Why not stay a little longer?"

She turned to Shen Si-wen and Shen Yen-li: "Don't you both agree?"

Both of them shrugged: "Either way works for us — nothing interesting to go back to anyway."

Shen Mingqiu knew how to read a room, and smiled agreeably: "Fifth Younger Sister and I are fine with it too."

Shen Weici closed her eyes a moment and conceded.

For the next two rounds — 'wind' and 'leaf' in turn — Shen Weici still let herself lose in the final round, when only she and Shen Zhao-zhao remained. She simply didn't want to drink the full three cups, and she didn't want to draw Shen Zhao-zhao's real resentment.

Shen Weici could hardly drink any more, so after losing she only drank the first cup and quietly poured the other two into her sleeve.

Shen Zhao-zhao's expression of triumph grew more pleased, and even her temper warmed during conversation.

When they were about to begin the next round, a maidservant came hurrying up the stairs from below. She glanced around the room, greeted the ladies, and then quickly made her way to Shen Weici's side and leaned in: "Third Miss, Master Zhang is here."

The maidservant's voice was very low, and the sound of rain and the chatter of everyone else covered it — no one else heard.

But Song Zhang, who had been lounging listlessly against the railing watching the rain, turned his head back and let his gaze settle on Shen Weici.

He watched her turn slightly, her wide sleeve resting decorously in her lap, her back presented to the room. Her posture was elegant, and in the quiet depths of her eyes something swirled — a feeling he could not quite read.

Then he saw her rise and step to a corner of the room, her back to everyone, leaving only a willowy dark-blue silhouette.

He looked away without interest.

Shen Weici asked the maidservant in a low voice: "Where is he now? Is he with my Father?"

The maidservant shook her head: "Master Zhang has just come from the Second Master's quarters. He is now waiting at the gate of the young miss's courtyard."

"I asked him to come inside and sit in the hall, but he said since you were not there, it wouldn't be proper to go in. He said he would wait outside until you returned."

Shen Weici heard this and nodded. She told the maidservant to go back, and added a reminder that the wind outside was cold and the rain was heavy — please bring him a cup of hot tea to warm him up.

The girl quietly acknowledged this and hurried off.

Shen Weici turned back and, seeing everyone's eyes on her, went over and said quietly: "Something has come up with a maidservant back in my courtyard. I need to go see to it. I'll join everyone again next time."

Someone asked: "What happened to the maidservant?"

Shen Weici smiled: "Only a small thing — a quarrel of sorts. I'll go and look into it."

Shen Zhao-zhao looked at Shen Weici: "And you have to manage something so trivial yourself?"

"Or is it that you can't bear to lose?"

That remark was a dig about the dice game — Shen Zhao-zhao had been nursing that grievance, and saying it aloud now finally gave her some relief.

Shen Weici looked at Shen Zhao-zhao, her eyes still quiet and serene: "I truly am no match for Second Elder Sister. But there is indeed something in the courtyard, and I did not mean to ruin everyone's mood. I'll come and make it up to Second Elder Sister another time."

Shen Zhao-zhao, seeing Shen Weici make herself small before her, felt her air of superiority deepen, and waved her off impatiently: "Go then, go."

Shen Weici gathered her sleeves and walked toward the stairs.

Song Zhang looked down from the window above. Before long, on the stone bridge below, Shen Weici appeared — a pale umbrella in hand, a white cloak around her shoulders, moving along the curved path with slow, careful steps. She passed through a blur of banana leaves and was gone.

From behind him, a murmur: "Third Younger Sister really is lovely — and such a gentle temper too. I think her breeding and bearing are not behind any well-born young lady. She might well make a fine match one day."

Shen Si-wen turned to look at Shen Zhao-zhao: "I hear Third Younger Cousin has come of age. Second Aunt, has she begun looking for a match?"

Shen Zhao-zhao's smile was cold: "She may have a pretty face — but she's still dragging around country habits underneath it. What good family would want her?"

"They'll find her any old match here in the capital and she should consider herself lucky. It'll be better than anything she would've found in Yuyang — she ought to be grateful."

Song Zhang looked at the empty distance where the figure had long since disappeared, then stood from his place against the railing and walked out with long strides.

Shen Zhao-zhao saw Song Zhang leave without so much as a word of farewell and wanted to call after him, but stopped herself.

Song Zhang did as he pleased. No one dared question it. From the start he had almost never stayed in this estate, and today had been the rare occasion he had come and eaten with them — though not for very long.

Shen Mingqiu watched Song Zhang's retreating back disappear and said to the others: "Song Elder Brother must be almost twenty-two now — do you think they're looking for a match for him?"

Shen Si-wen shook his head: "Second Elder Brother is a cold one. He's only been back in the capital a little over a year, and already no shortage of women have thrown themselves at him. Probably Aunty is looking into it."

"Apparently a few days ago some woman deliberately stepped in front of his carriage just to get his attention."

Shen Mingqiu asked curiously: "And then what happened?"

Shen Si-wen clicked his tongue: "Then Second Elder Brother had the carriage drive straight over her. They say she'll never walk right again."

Everyone in the room drew a sharp breath.

chapters.title: A Solemn Intention
chapters.content:
Before Shen Weici had even reached the gate of her courtyard, she spotted the dark green of Zhang Yuanheng's robe from a distance — a tall, upright figure standing under the eave of the gate, straight as a pine.

In the rain and mist, white threads of water vapor rose around everything, blurring the world into pale vagueness. But that figure grew clearer by degrees as she approached, and she could feel, even from this distance, the weight of his eyes on her.

She lowered her lashes, lifted her skirt, and walked up to stand before him.

"Why didn't Master Zhang come inside to sit?"

Zhang Yuanheng's gaze remained fixed on her, taking in her cool yet gentle expression: "Third Miss is still living under her family's roof. For me to go inside — it would violate propriety, and I feared it might invite people to talk."

Shen Weici smiled faintly and looked up at him: "Master Zhang has already seen my Father, I take it?"

Zhang Yuanheng smiled back: "I saw Minister Shen first. It was actually someone from his quarters who brought me here."

Shen Weici glanced at the young manservant standing nearby — one of her father's most reliable attendants from the study. That was reassuring. No one could say anything untoward.

The tall figure of Zhang Yuanheng before her radiated a quiet warmth. Three steps separated them, and yet Shen Weici felt, at that moment, inexplicably at ease.

She asked again: "Did Master Zhang come with something to say?"

Zhang Yuanheng looked into the eyes looking up at him — misty, like the rain itself. His own cheeks grew warm, and he felt like a young boy struck by his first feeling — slightly at a loss for words in front of a fifteen-year-old girl.

He smiled inwardly at himself, and held out the small box he had been carrying: "What Third Miss said the other day — I went home and thought about it carefully. I also consulted my father. He has agreed."

"I came today specifically to see Third Miss, hoping to make my intentions more evident — so Third Miss will know I am not a man who speaks carelessly. Having made a promise, I wished to make it in person, and let Third Miss be at ease."

In truth, when Zhang Yuanheng had been waiting at the courtyard gate, he had looked over the whole courtyard. The position of the place was clearly out of the way — and the courtyard itself was old, lichen creeping along the walls, the pillars faded and unrepaired, the courtyard bricks crumbling underfoot. He could scarcely believe that a household as grand as this Marquis estate could arrange quarters like this for a young lady.

He had met Minister Shen twice now, and the man had spoken of Shen Weici as a daughter he cherished. Yet if he truly cherished her — why was she placed here?

He looked at Shen Weici, and his heart only grew more earnest. She had endured all of this, yet remained gentle and quiet through it all, the only sign of inner sorrow a faint shadow deep in her eyes — no complaints, no grievances on display. He was deeply drawn to her, and wanted to do all that he could for her.

The sound of Zhang Yuanheng's voice came to her again: "Everything else I have to say is written in the letter inside. Please accept it, Third Miss."

The box in her hands still held the faint warmth of his. She tightened her fingers around it, then looked up at him: "I will go home and read it carefully."

Zhang Yuanheng smiled, and then he noticed it — the pink flush on Shen Weici's porcelain cheeks and the delicate trace of fruit wine on her breath. That soft, warm fragrance mingled with her own, and his throat moved. Without quite meaning to, his body leaned an inch closer. His gaze lingered on the lowered lashes of her eyes.

The lashes were very long, and when he looked more closely, the tip of her nose seemed to carry a slight sheen of moisture — as if mist had settled and left its trace.

His heart beat faster. He knew he ought to go. But his body did not want to leave.

He asked quietly: "Third Miss has been drinking fruit wine?"

Shen Weici felt him lean slightly toward her, though it was only by a fraction — not enough to make her feel he was overstepping.

She did not step back. She nodded and said softly: "I drank a few sips of warm wine just now at the pavilion."

Zhang Yuanheng also nodded, looking at her. She clearly could not hold her drink well — the outer corners of her eyes were tinged pink.

The slight upward tilt at those outer corners, the long lashes beneath them, the smoothness of her jaw — white, impossibly white.

He knew he had no reason to keep her talking. The rain was heavy, and he was worried about her frail constitution — that she might take in the cold if she stood out here too long. Pressing down the reluctance rising in his chest, he said: "The rain is cold, Third Miss. Please go back inside."

Shen Weici looked at Zhang Yuanheng. He was standing in front of her, beneath the eave, and she saw that he had been shielding her from a good portion of the rain blowing in. His sleeve was damp, and small droplets of rain clung to his hair.

Her heart moved. She looked at him again, and the warmth in his eyes was unmistakably genuine. He had surely noticed the state of her courtyard, too — and yet here he was, unchanged. That comforted her more than she expected.

It smoothed over the last trace of uneasy doubt she had been carrying.

She wanted to find a steady, reliable companion. She hoped Zhang Yuanheng would be that person — someone to whom she could give her trust, slowly and by degrees. Someone for whom she would bear children and keep a peaceful home.

There were a thousand things she could not put into words. She knew she would never be able to give herself entirely — that deep in her heart she would always keep a path back, something held in reserve, so that no matter how things ended, she might still find a way out.

She nodded, and said softly: "The road is slippery, Master Zhang — please take care on your way."

Zhang Yuanheng nodded, then looked at Shen Weici one last, long time. He took the umbrella his attendant held out, opened it, and walked into the rain.

But he had only gone two steps when he stopped and turned back, unable to help himself. Shen Weici was still standing under the eave, watching him go. Her eyes still held that cool, clear quality — but now, when he looked at them, he thought he could detect a thread of warmth.

She stood in her fine garments, dark hair loosely pinned, a few loose strands stirring in the wind — sweeping across her delicate shoulder, then gently across her cheek. And behind her, the sparse and quiet courtyard seemed at once out of place with her and perfectly matched — just like the faint melancholy in the depths of her eyes.

She was warm, yet somehow also cold.

He said quietly: "Third Miss, please go back. You needn't see me off."

Shen Weici smiled: "I will wait until Master Zhang has gone first."

Those words warmed Zhang Yuanheng's heart. The lingering, uncertain feeling that had unsettled him only moments before dissolved entirely. He smiled and, not wanting to make her stand outside any longer, finally turned away.

When Zhang Yuanheng's figure had faded into the distance, Shen Weici lowered her eyes to the box in her hands, and made to turn back inside.

Her head was swimming badly, and the wind sent a fresh ache through it. The fruit wine was catching up to her, and she felt a wave of exhaustion. She was thinking of lying down for a while.

But just as she turned, the corner of her eye caught a flash of red — Song Zhang, in a scarlet robe, passing by with a black umbrella. He looked as though he was simply walking past, as though by chance — and yet stopped exactly in front of her courtyard gate.

Shen Weici paused and looked at Song Zhang, standing there in the rain.

He still wore the black-and-gold sword at his hip, a gold crown binding his hair, two daggers thrust through his waistband, jade pendants at his belt, and gold thread glinting in the pattern of his robe — an aura of cold, imposing authority that pressed down simply by standing there.

chapters.title: He Had Underestimated Her
chapters.content:
Rain streamed from the eaves like a curtain, a transparent net hanging between the two of them.

Shen Weici said nothing. She waited for Song Zhang to speak.

He looked as though he had come to say something. She had already turned it over in her mind several times.

Song Zhang studied Shen Weici for a moment — his detached, indifferent gaze moving over the box in her hand, then settling on the flush of color in her cheeks.

That soft pink was vivid against her skin, carrying a faint, diffused warmth. He had just watched her stand beside Zhang Yuanheng like a small bird nestling close, head tilted, a shy blush coloring her face — a glimpse of spring warmth.

For some reason, Song Zhang found that image inexplicably irritating. He gave Shen Weici a contemptuous, mocking look — and walked on without a word.

He had thought her somewhat different from other women. But she was simply another woman trying to climb higher in the world. She had barely been in the household a month, and had already managed to catch herself a man.

He had watched clearly just now — she had stood at the courtyard gate, gazing after Zhang Yuanheng with undisguised tenderness, until she had thoroughly bewitched him.

Zhang Yuanheng was normally the most self-controlled and principled man the Emperor had around him — upright, never fawning, never demeaning himself. Even the Emperor had spoken well of him. And yet just now, in front of Shen Weici, the man had been dazed with infatuation, his soul apparently stolen clean away.

Song Zhang thought he had truly underestimated Shen Weici. He was not sure what arts of beauty she practiced.

Shen Weici noticed Song Zhang's gaze returning, again and again, to the object in her hand — that mocking contempt in his eyes impossible to miss.

He had seen what had happened just now between her and Zhang Yuanheng. He had probably drawn the worst possible conclusion.

But Shen Weici believed her own conduct had been proper. Her father's attendant had been present the whole time — nothing that happened could be considered improper. If Song Zhang wanted to make something of it, that was his own distorted thinking. She herself was here to find a suitable husband, after all.

Zhang Yuanheng had feelings for her, and she did for him as well.

That was nothing shameful.

With that thought settled, Shen Weici no longer looked at Song Zhang, and turned back into her courtyard.

Back inside, the hem of her skirt was entirely wet, and she had stood out in the rain for a good while. The cold was seeping through her again.

Yuedeng brought fresh clothes and helped her change. Shen Weici put them on, went to recline on the daybed, pulled a light quilt over herself, and only then opened Zhang Yuanheng's box.

The box was not large, but far more delicately crafted than the previous one.

She unfastened the silver clasp. On top was a letter.

Shen Weici lowered her eyes and unfolded the paper. Zhang Yuanheng had written his commitment in solemn terms, and promised to arrange for the formal proposal to be made before the new year if possible — and no later than shortly after.

At the end, she came upon a few lines of restrained feeling. Her slender fingers traced over those characters, and Zhang Yuanheng's warm, composed eyes rose up in her mind.

He was like a gentleman who kept perfect command of himself. Even in writing that he could not sleep for thinking of her, he immediately followed it with a note that he hoped she would forgive him for being too forward.

Shen Weici turned it over. She remembered that Zhang Yuanheng must be twenty-four — quite a bit older than she was. Yet this careful, tentative tenderness moved her nonetheless.

She folded the letter neatly and asked Yuedeng to put it away with the earlier ones.

Then she looked at what lay resting quietly inside the box — a jade pendant and a pair of earrings — and lifted them up to examine them.

The white jade pendant had not a single flaw. Zhang Yuanheng had written that this piece of jade had been given by his father to his mother in earlier years. When he heard that Zhang Yuanheng had someone in his heart, his father had taken out this matched set as a token of sincerity.

The jade pendant dangled from a red cord before her eyes. She sat with her head tilted slightly, gazing at it in the candlelight, her head still aching and swimming. She wanted to look at it a little longer.

Yuedeng beside her was equally transfixed: "Is this from Master Zhang? It's beautiful."

Shen Weici looked at the jade in silence for a long moment, then smiled.

Finally she looked at the pair of smoky-green jadeite earrings. Zhang Yuanheng had written that he came across them by chance and felt they would suit her, so he had bought them for her.

The earrings were neither too large nor too small, and in the lamplight the smoky color was both luminous and lovely. Even Yuedeng stared at them in a daze.

Shen Weici looked at them for a good while before asking Chuntao to put both the jade pendant and the box away together in a safe place.

She curled herself up on the bed, tired to the bone, and coughed twice. Outside it was raining and cold, and her body had begun to protest.

Yuedeng put everything away, then crouched down beside Shen Weici again: "Why does it feel even colder here in the winter?"

"The rain has made it worse. Is your knee all right, miss? I'll go heat some water over the brazier outside and fill the warming stone."

She rose to see to it.

The room was quiet, only Shen Weici left inside. The carved screen separated the inner chamber from the outer. She propped her head on her hand, dizzy, and thought to herself that she clearly could not drink — fruit wine was just as intoxicating as any other.

She had been utterly exhausted and ready to fall asleep, yet the aching in her knee kept nagging at her. She placed her palm over it, and the cold seemed to pull away every last shred of warmth her hand had left.

By the time Chuntao came in with the warming stone, Shen Weici had fallen asleep against the daybed.

Chuntao moved with the quietest possible steps, slid the warming stone in, helped Shen Weici out of her outer robe, tucked the quilt around her properly, and then tiptoed back out.

Meanwhile, Song Zhang had walked some distance past Shen Weici's courtyard before abruptly turning on his heel — only to find the gate standing empty, no one there.

He was reminded of the fact that when he heard Zhang Yuanheng was coming, he had somehow followed along this whole stretch of path for no clear reason. What did it matter to him whom Shen Weici saw?

If he kept on this path, he would either reach the rear side gate or end up in the back garden.

The attendant behind him dared not speak, but then Song Zhang's sharp gaze cut toward him: "Your master has walked the wrong way and you can't even say so?"

Minhe, who served this ancestor of a master with his life constantly at stake, dropped to one knee immediately: "It is this one's failure. I deserve the General's punishment."

Song Zhang gave a cold snort, turned with a sweep of his sleeve, and reversed his steps back toward the East Courtyard.

Minhe let out a quiet breath of relief and followed, carefully and cautiously.

Song Zhang returned to his courtyard. He had barely stepped inside the gate when he found a small, delicate maidservant waiting beneath the covered walkway outside the main room.

She had red lips and white teeth, eyes like clear autumn water — vivid and beautiful, with a high, full figure and a slender waist. The moment she saw him walk in, she came toward him like water flowing over stone.

Song Zhang had been around more women than he could count. In the capital — the pleasure houses, the flower boats — there was scarcely a place that did not know him. Women throwing themselves at him were countless. But no one in his own courtyard had ever been so bold.

He flung the umbrella to a waiting servant and stared at the maidservant with a blank, emotionless face, fingers closing around her chin: "Who sent you?"

The girl was terrified by his expression and stumbled out her answer: "It... it was the Commandery Princess who sent me."

"She said the Second Young Master had no one to warm his bed, and asked me to come and attend to the Second Young Master properly."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. His expression remained cold. He released his grip and stepped into the room.

He settled back into the rosewood chair, resting one hand on the armrest. He accepted the hot tea a servant brought and, looking at the maidservant who had followed him inside, let an icy, faint contempt settle into his gaze.

His dark eyes gave nothing away: "And how do you plan to attend to me?"

The maidservant's cheeks flushed crimson. She gave him a long, inviting look, and then knelt on the floor and began to crawl toward him.

Her soft body moved with practiced undulation, her slender white hands settling on Song Zhang's thigh. She glanced up at him with a shy look, then bent her head and ducked beneath his outer robe.

Song Zhang looked down, and let out a scoffing sound: "Interesting."

His mother had certainly gone to some effort.

The other maidservants in the room did not dare look. They immediately averted their eyes, retreating to the corners — but in the next moment, they all heard a sharp cry of pain.

chapters.title: The Anger He Directed at Her
chapters.content:
By now the sky had grown faintly dark. Song Zhang sat with one leg crossed over the other, the raised toe of his boot tapping steadily against the chin of the maidservant kneeling and trembling on the floor.

His black satin boot knocked at her once, then again — smearing its sole's dust across what had been a smooth, pretty face.

His voice was languid, low: "You came to attend to me, and this is all you're capable of?"

"When you go back to my mother, you'll know what to tell her?"

The maidservant immediately dropped into a series of rapid, desperate bows: "This servant knows, knows exactly what to say — please spare this servant's life, Second Young Master."

Song Zhang's earlier kick had driven straight into her solar plexus, sending blood surging to her throat. She had thought for an instant she would be killed on the spot — she was certainly not going to try that again with this man.

The Commandery Princess had sent her here to find out whether the Second Young Master was incapable. But she had just seen for herself that there was nothing incapable about him — she simply was not up to the task.

Song Zhang looked at the maidservant kowtowing on the floor, found the rhythmic knocking sound irritating, and sent her out with another kick to the shoulder.

Song Zhang had always had a fastidious nature. His trousers had been mouthed by that maidservant, and the thought revolted him. He rose and called for hot water to bathe.

The water was ready quickly. Song Zhang leaned against the edge of the bath, tilted his head back, and let a maidservant scrub him down.

Steam rose all around. He closed his eyes with a sigh of comfort.

But in the moment his eyes shut, the image that rose before him was Shen Weici's face — flushed with wine color, standing before Zhang Yuanheng with that faint, shy warmth — peach-pink at her cheeks like a breeze of spring had moved through.

He clenched his jaw and snapped his eyes open. He stared at the hot water lapping at his chest, and then the memory of that warmth between his fingers surfaced — Shen Weici's slight tilt of the head.

He was dazed for an instant. Then a heat rushed through him, and with a sharp, furious movement he shot to his feet from the bath.

He had no peace even soaking in a bath.

He was going right now to see what manner of creature this Shen Weici actually was. Or perhaps she had secretly used some trick on him too — bewitching him the same way she had apparently bewitched Zhang Yuanheng.

Water splashed loudly across the floor. The maidservant inside the bathing room was so startled she tumbled backward onto the floor, and when she raised her head again, the bathing room was empty.

Song Zhang called for servants to help him dress, left the sword behind, and walked out with a cold expression.

Minhe, standing guard at the door, saw Song Zhang walking out again, and quickly stepped forward: "Is the General heading to the Palace?"

"This one will go and have a carriage prepared."

Song Zhang's step paused. He looked at Minhe: "No need."
