That matter was the reason Shen Rongshen had been entirely compliant with Lady Wen over the years, and had kept to the promise made to her father — that he would not take a concubine without her agreement.

It was also why he had not dared bring Shen Weici's mother back to the capital.

Lady Wen was fiery and jealous, unable to tolerate any woman near him. In the first two years of their marriage he had managed to restrain himself, but afterward the desire to take a concubine had stirred — he had actually brought a woman home to kowtow before Lady Wen, and been thrown out flat, Lady Wen refusing absolutely.

Only during his time as Educational Commissioner had he been able to breathe, and it was there that he had encountered Shen Weici's mother and allowed his suppressed desires to surface.

He thought too of how Lady Wen, going back to her family, would certainly go to complain to her father. Her father's official rank was only one grade above his, and her grandfather had long since left the court — but if old business was truly brought up, the fault would lie with him.

His gaze returned to Shen Weici, standing to one side. His head ached. He looked at her with exhaustion: "Go back."

Shen Weici looked at her father, saw the fatigue in his eyes, and stepped forward quietly: "Father — a little hardship on my part is nothing."

"I don't want to cause difficulty for Father anymore. Please don't let things between you and the Second Lady grow strained on my account from now on."

"I never intended to make things hard for Father."

Shen Rongshen took a long breath, his body slightly hunched. He gently patted Shen Weici's shoulder and asked quietly of this sensible daughter: "Are you truly not aggrieved?"

Shen Weici shook her head: "I am not."

"Knowing Father cares for me — daughter is already content."

Shen Rongshen was struck by these words. His gaze dropped to the faint scratch on Shen Weici's jaw from Shen Zhaozhao's fingernail, and guilt churned in him. He felt, for the moment, rather useless.

He had still not done right by her.

He said quietly: "You needn't think about what's happened here — just go back. Tomorrow morning, you also needn't go to pay your respects. Your stepmother won't hold it against you."

Shen Weici understood that her continued presence here was no longer appropriate. She pressed her fingernails into her palm and murmured assent.

She looked at her father once more, then turned and walked out of the courtyard.

She paused in the yard and glanced back. She saw her father lift the curtain and go inside — the sound of apologetic, placating words reached her faintly — and she turned her gaze away again.

Outside the gate, the autumn wind was desolate. She looked up at the heavy, overcast sky, and without knowing why, her eyes felt hot — nor did she know why, in this moment, her heart had found no peace.

Fortunately the sky was dark, and a few loose strands of hair had fallen over her face. No one would see the light in her eyes.

From behind her came murmuring voices and several indeterminate glances. Shen Weici did not care to listen closely — whatever was being said would not be anything kind.

Walking alone along the flagstone path, damp dew sweeping against the hem of her skirt, she only looked silently down at her feet.

Song Zhang was coming from the other direction. From quite a distance away he spotted Shen Weici alone ahead of him.

He stopped where he was. His phoenix eyes narrowed toward her. The slender, fragile figure moved very slowly, her head always lowered, the peach-pink skirt shifting faintly — as though she might topple at any moment.

The soft, warm fragrance that belonged to her drifted over. Song Zhang looked at the figure now only a few paces away, and made no move to step aside. He simply looked at her with furrowed brows — at the thin scratch mark on her cheek, and the lost look in her eyes.

The fallen strands of her hair lifted in the breeze. The silver pin in her dark hair flickered faintly.

Her eyes were full of moisture.

He pressed his lips together.

Shen Weici saw the pair of black boots blocking her path and paused. She raised her face, saw it was Song Zhang, then lowered her eyes and moved aside.

She said nothing — quietly stepping out of the way, her lashes blinking steadily, as if holding back tears. She turned her head slightly to one side, casting a soft shadow beneath her eyes.

This time Song Zhang did not make things difficult for her. He walked past — yet halted again a step behind her, watching as she walked on.

Up ahead, Yuedeng's anxious figure came hurrying over. Seeing Shen Weici, she immediately wiped her eyes: "Miss — did they bully you again?"

Shen Weici patted the back of Yuedeng's hand and said hoarsely: "Never mind. Let's go back."

Yuedeng's tears kept coming. She wiped them: "Those old matrons stomped all the charcoal to pieces — not a single whole lump left. It's too much."

Shen Weici said nothing. She held Yuedeng's hand tight and walked on in silence.

Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici's retreating figure and remembered the small red mark on her jaw — vivid against the pale-glowing whiteness of her cheek.

Minhe stood to one side. He watched his General stand motionless, staring after Third Young Miss's figure — not sure what he was looking at.

Others might not have noticed the General's strangeness these recent days — but Minhe had noticed it all too well.

In the past, Song Zhang would at the very least stay at the palace to have a meal with the Emperor, or play a round of chess before leaving. Or he would take his inner circle of men to the pleasure quarters to drink, with a few beautiful women for entertainment.

Especially in those first days back in the capital — there was barely a pleasure house in the city that didn't know the General's face. After ten-odd years of restraint in the military camps, returning home, he'd cut loose with the trusted men who'd come back with him.

Just canter his horse down East Willow Street and the girls upstairs would be calling out welcomes.

But now he was back at the Manor early every evening. Some nights when he came back late, he'd deliberately enter through the West Gate and take the long way around through the East Compound — wasn't that just to pass that particular courtyard and steal a look?

In the past he would stay at the Manor four or five days a month at most. Now it had been half a month of going back early night after night — the manor guards had also been reduced in number.

His men had to come to the Manor just to make their reports.

Minhe was beginning to think — could it be that his General had actually developed some kind of feeling for Third Young Miss?

That General — the one who wouldn't look twice at all those noble young ladies throwing themselves at him. The cold demon king who, when the barbarian kingdoms on the border sent him their beauties stripped bare, simply had them kicked out. If that General were to stir in the heart — what on earth would that even look like?

Minhe scarcely dared imagine it.

Song Zhang looked a moment longer in the direction of the Second Branch, frowning as he thought about how Shen Weici had ignored him just now, and felt discomfort stir in his chest again.

But then he thought of the moisture in her eyes, and a faint, agitated impulse arose in him — the impulse to vent her grievance for her.

Song Zhang felt he had truly been bewitched by that woman, and could not figure out what method she had used on him. Any man who looked at her seemed unable to look away.

Was it that perpetually fragile, pitiable air of hers?

Song Zhang clasped his hands behind his back, forcing himself not to think of that face, and turned to stride away.

chapters.title: Inquiring About Linchun Courtyard
chapters.content:
Back at Linchun Courtyard, the offending matrons had already gone. Shen Weici looked at the mess strewn across the courtyard. The three maids were sweeping up the crushed charcoal from the ground, and every one of them looked anxiously at her when she came in.

They could not go without heat through winter.

Shen Weici pressed her lips together and walked to the inner room.

Once inside, Yuedeng saw Shen Weici sit on the daybed and stare blankly down at the still-burning brazier, then noticed the scratch mark on Shen Weici's jaw.

She hurried to press a cup of warming tea into Shen Weici's hands, then went to fetch medicine and apply it to the wound, her eyes reddening as she did: "That Shen Zhaozhao — she's no better than a common shrew. What behavior is this for a daughter of a great family?"

"Did Miss say anything about it to the Second Lord just now?"

Shen Weici closed her eyes: "This is not the moment to say it."

Yuedeng looked at Shen Weici's cheek and paused: "Why not?"

Shen Weici cupped her fingers around the teacup, lowered her head, and drank a sip. The steam bloomed warmly against her face, spreading a faint blush of color across it.

"Father got into a quarrel with the Second Lady on my behalf. I cannot add fuel to the fire."

Yuedeng said: "Add fuel to the fire — good! Best if the Second Lord sees clearly how the Second Lady and Shen Zhaozhao have been treating Miss all this time."

Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng with a wry smile: "Do you think Father doesn't know? He must have found out about the seamstress's garments long ago — and yet he never mentioned it, never thought to have me new clothing made. He was planning to let it pass quietly. These things are never as simple as you make them sound."

"When I was in the Second Branch just now, I only heard a few words — but Father can't hold out long in the face of the Second Lady's forcefulness. That Father stood up for me this time, I think, is partly because of my connection with Master Zhang. Now that Father knows I may be going to the Earldom, he has begun to take me a little more seriously."

"And partly he does feel some guilt toward me."

"But because Father stood up for me this once doesn't mean he can stand up for me in every matter. The only one who can shelter me here, in any small way, is Father — but Father is away in the daytime, and the Second Lady has far too many ways to make my life difficult."

Shen Weici exhaled slowly and lowered her lashes: "In truth I never expected Father to go and confront the Second Lady. Now that the scene has become hard to resolve, I have become a thorn in the flesh of the Manor. I can't stay here long."

Yuedeng asked faintly: "Then what will Miss do?"

Shen Weici looked toward the darkening dusk, and in the dimness looked at Yuedeng: "I am alone. The only solution is to have the Zhang family come and propose as soon as possible."

Yuedeng lowered her head and thought: "Should Miss write a letter to Master Zhang — tell him about her difficulties and urge him to come sooner?"

Shen Weici shook her head: "If I tell him of my difficulties, it's as though I'm forcing his hand. I don't want that."

Yuedeng was troubled: "Then what can be done?"

Shen Weici looked at her: "Many solutions are found only as you go. I've been through so much to get here, and in truth most of it has never felt truly unbearable to me."

"Because I ask for neither wealth nor fame, neither flawless devotion nor perfection — only stability. Though that is not easily found, it is not impossibly hard either."

"Marriage is one way I am seeking stability. But if marriage in the end cannot give me stability, I can always find my own way."

Yuedeng had been with Shen Weici since she was seven years old and knew her history better than anyone. The nearest family they had, the very people who should have loved them most, had done things more wicked than even the Second Lady. Compared to that, this truly had not reached those depths.

She asked: "But without charcoal — how to get through the winter?"

Shen Weici reached out and pointed to the box still sitting on the table: "Inside that box is the fur collar Young Lord Xu sent. In a few days the Second Lady has said we're going to a banquet — when we come back, remember to bring it and pawn it on the way. Use the money to buy charcoal."

Yuedeng saw the sense in it. She looked around: "But what about these few days in the meantime?"

Shen Weici smiled: "Didn't we survive them in Yuyang?"

Yuedeng wiped her eyes: "Yuyang wasn't this cold."

Shen Weici set down her teacup and held her fingers over the nearly spent charcoal: "Tell the maids to go to bed early these next few nights. There's no need to come and wait on me."

Yuedeng murmured quietly in agreement.

Meanwhile, Song Zhang had barely returned to his own rooms when a matron was waiting, asking him to go to the Princess Consort's quarters.

Song Zhang all but ignored her and walked past.

The matron saw Song Zhang's retreating figure — she had long expected this reception — and hurried to call the maid behind her to follow, chasing after him: "The Princess Consort has selected several young ladies of suitable age for you. Old servant has brought the portrait scrolls — won't you at least look?"

Song Zhang glanced at Matron Xing, then at the portrait scrolls the maid behind her was carrying. His eyes were unambiguously impatient. He looked at Minhe once, then walked into his main hall.

Minhe understood the instruction and, with a mixture of coaxing and polite firmness, escorted the matron out of the courtyard.

Inside, Song Zhang leaned against the back of his chair, long legs propped on the table, and looked out the window. He said to the entering Minhe: "Go and find out what happened in Linchun Courtyard this afternoon."

Minhe's jaw nearly fell open. The General — actually beginning to pay attention to these small domestic matters.

Well. The General had not been himself for a while now.

By the time Minhe came back to report, Song Zhang had just stepped out of the bathing room. Those habitually cold phoenix eyes turned on him once, and Minhe's whole body broke out in goosebumps.

He watched Song Zhang take a black wool-lined robe from the clothes rack and sling it on, then walk to the writing desk, sit down, and begin opening the letters from his subordinates. Minhe hurried over and stood at his side, speaking quietly: "Your subordinate found out. It was a small matter."

"Just a question of a few catties of charcoal."

He paused, watching the undisturbed look on Song Zhang's face, still on his letters, and continued: "Apparently the Second Lady had told the housekeeper to withhold Linchun Courtyard's charcoal — only five catties was sent. The Second Lord somehow found out this afternoon and came home to quarrel with the Second Lady."

"Oh — and before that, the clothing the seamstress made for Third Young Miss didn't fit properly. The Second Lord felt the Second Lady was being harsh toward Third Young Miss, and the quarrel got quite heated. He even said he'd repudiate the Second Lady."

"Then Second Young Miss brought some matrons and went and stomped all the charcoal in Linchun Courtyard flat — they say she also struck someone and dragged Third Young Miss off to the Second Branch to beg forgiveness. Quite the uproar."

"Now the Second Lord and the Second Lady have both been summoned by the Old Madam. A number of maids saw the whole thing — the Old Madam probably knows by now."

Song Zhang said nothing. He opened the next letter with an expression of smooth unconcern.

These days, the capital's Feathered Guard patrol reports were presented daily to the Middle Guard Commander, who then submitted them to the General.

He thought of how the Emperor had summoned the General back to the capital, and how unwillingly the General had returned to be installed in this post. The work was undemanding enough — but now he had become something more like a civilian official. Other than going to the training grounds to spar with his men, the days here truly lacked the freedom of the border.

With the General at the border, the surrounding small kingdoms had not dared act out of turn. Wine and beauties had been sent in an endless variety, and he could do as he liked. Back in the capital, he was constrained at every side.

The letters piled thick on the desk — large and small matters from inside and outside the palace, including the movements of the imperial princes — all of it in there.

Song Zhang finished the last letter. It was deep into the night.

His fingers tapped the desk as he turned over in his hand a letter concerning the Second Prince, then held it to the candle flame and let it burn away completely.

chapters.title: Summoned by the Old Madam
chapters.content:
The moon was at its height. Song Zhang waved Minhe out of the room and leaned back in his chair — and once again found his thoughts drifting to Shen Weici.

He had been thinking of her, on and off, for days now — like a spell he could not shake.

He looked out at the night sky, then thought again of her dazed face earlier, and the scratch mark beneath her jaw.

His tall body rose from the chair. He could not say why, but he felt that going for a look was the only thing that would settle the restless irritation in his chest.

Over something as trivial as a few catties of charcoal — the Second Branch was truly laughable.

He stopped the attempt Minhe made to follow and went out into the night alone.

Linchun Courtyard looked even more desolate by night. The courtyard was very quiet — not even a gate maid posted outside, only two lanterns burning under the covered walkway.

With his skill, entering a woman's private chamber presented no obstacle, especially with not a single maid anywhere in the courtyard — no one even keeping night watch. He could not imagine how anyone in her courtyard could be so remiss in their duties.

Then he thought of Shen Weici's gentle, good-natured face, the quiet way she avoided sharpness in front of Shen Zhaozhao — and understood something of her difficulty.

The room was cold. In the dim candlelight, he could see only the charcoal brazier, its warmth long extinguished.

Song Zhang's gaze moved past the brazier and settled on Shen Weici.

Her body was curled the same slight way as before. Her face was buried deep in the bedding. She lay on her side with propriety, the covers pulled tight and neat.

His steps drew him, unbidden, to her bedside. Song Zhang sat on the edge of the bed and studied the sleeping face of Shen Weici, turning over in his mind why she always managed to attract his attention.

The fine scratch on her jaw was still visible. Song Zhang took a flask of medicine from his robe and dabbed it onto the wound.

Her skin was like white mutton-fat jade — smooth and soft. His long fingers slid, as if of their own accord, to the curve of her face.

Song Zhang's hands were full of calluses from years of holding a sword. The roughness of his fingers seemed to disturb her — she did not wake, but gave a faint frown.

Both brows, finely curved as painted willows, furrowed in an expression of delicate distress.

Song Zhang looked at her and froze. His tall, lean body leaned forward involuntarily, and his warm breath fell against her. He looked at the lips before him — slightly parted — and something moved in his throat.

That warm, lovely fragrance was powerfully tempting. Song Zhang nearly lost all reason.

He was no stranger to what passed between men and women, and had never before felt an impulse like this.

Song Zhang was not the sort of man to shrink from anything — but pride made it all the less acceptable to him that he should develop feelings for a woman who played her arts on every man around her.

Especially a woman who, in the presence of another man, had been shy and tender, full of soft feeling.

He paused for a long moment, restrained the impulse to pull that soft body into his arms, stood, and left in long strides.

But after he returned, every time Song Zhang closed his eyes he imagined he could smell that fragrance, and felt the urge to go near her again. He tossed and turned, and the heat within him only burned hotter.

---

The next morning, Shen Weici did not wake particularly early. Her father had told her she need not go to Lady Wen that day, and she had no intention of going.

It was a rare pleasure to burrow in the bedding and refuse to surface — nothing could have made her put out so much as a single finger in the cold air.

So this was how cold the capital was. Just barely into winter and already this bitter.

She lay looking at the bed curtains, listening to the sounds from beyond the curtain, and turned her head to look.

Yuedeng came in with a face full of delight and sat down at Shen Weici's bedside, saying excitedly: "Miss, this morning when Hexia came in she found a large sack of charcoal on the covered walkway!"

"It must be the Second Lord who found out about Second Miss coming yesterday and had more sent to you."

Shen Weici gave a start: "Is that so? Did anyone see who brought it?"

Yuedeng shook her head: "The person who brought it wasn't seen. But in the whole Manor, who besides the Second Lord would have charcoal sent to Miss?"

"And such a large sack — just left on the walkway. This is the only courtyard in this part of the Manor. It couldn't have been left at the wrong place."

That seemed reasonable.

As they spoke, two maids came in smiling, carrying two braziers of burning charcoal and setting them beside the bed, saying: "This charcoal seems even better than the last batch — burns without noise or smoke. Miss won't be cold anymore."

The moment the braziers came in, a wave of warmth breathed through the damp, cold room. Shen Weici felt a small greed for that warmth. Back in Yuyang, having one brazier like this to burn through a winter's day had been a rare luxury.

She had barely finished breakfast after getting up when a servant came to say the Old Madam was asking her to come.

The Old Madam asking for her this early in the morning — she thought it was almost certainly about yesterday's events.

Shen Weici tidied herself briefly, had Yuedeng drape a cloak over her shoulders, and made her way to the Old Madam's West Small Courtyard.

The Renshou Hall was Shen Weici's first visit. The matron at the door was surprisingly warm and smiled as she showed her inside.

The heated chamber was running a floor-warmer, and it was pleasantly warm the moment she entered. Shen Weici saw Lady Wen and Shen Zhaozhao already with the Old Madam, and quickly removed her cloak to go and greet the Old Madam and Lady Wen.

Shen Weici's face was composed and respectful, as though yesterday's events had not occurred at all.

Old Madam Shen looked at the demurely lowered eyes before her and smiled, drawing Shen Weici to sit beside her. She took her hand and asked: "Coming into the Marquis Manor — has it been difficult for you?"

Hearing this, Shen Weici understood that the Old Madam must have learned about yesterday, and hurriedly rose with a somewhat flustered expression: "Weici is grateful to the Old Madam and stepmother for taking her in. Weici does not feel it has been difficult — Weici cherishes every day she has here."

The Old Madam smiled at Shen Weici — she had a way with words — and drew her back down to sit, then said gently: "There's no need to be nervous. I've already heard about yesterday."

"I've learned the full details. Your stepmother had no intention of treating you harshly — it was simply the servants below taking advantage of your mild nature to withhold your charcoal for their own use."

"Those servants who had no eyes have already been sent to receive their punishment. You can rest easy — nothing like this will happen again."

She then looked at Lady Wen: "In future, handle Weici's needs yourself — don't leave everything to the servants. And stop letting such small things cause quarrels with Rongshen."

"And don't go running back to your family home over every little thing."

Lady Wen received the Old Madam's sharp look and nodded repeatedly: "Mother may rest easy. Daughter-in-law has taken note — this time was Daughter-in-law's poor management."

Shen Zhaozhao, watching her mother admit fault before her grandmother, thought of the slap her own father had given her yesterday, looked away, and shot a covert glare at Shen Weici, her expression sour.

All because they wanted to marry her off to Zhang Tingyi — why were they showing Shen Weici this good face? If she refused to go, she could always be bound and dragged there.

Shen Zhaozhao was still inwardly unresigned when she was startled to hear her grandmother's voice address her sternly. She turned to find the grandmother who was usually so gentle and loving looking at her with clear reproach: "You are also not to bully your sister again. You nearly left a scar on your sister's face — if it happens once more, I will punish you as well."

"Settle yourself and wait to be married to Zhi'an next year — stop stirring up trouble."

Shen Zhaozhao felt aggrieved inside. She gripped her embroidered handkerchief tight and gave a reluctant but obedient nod.

Shen Weici listened in silence to all this performance — and gradually something dubious stirred in her heart.

chapters.title: Intercepting Her Letter
chapters.content:
This doubt had actually begun the moment Shen Weici entered the Manor.

Among everyone in the Marquis Manor, the two people who showed her any care at all were her father — and the Old Madam.

It was the Old Madam who had intervened with Lady Wen to take her in, and who maintained a surface show of looking after her whenever something happened.

Yet this protection was always light and evasive — nothing that actually penalized Lady Wen or Shen Zhaozhao in any meaningful way. The Old Madam's words just now had even been offered as explanation and excuse on Lady Wen's behalf.

Just like last time with the Shuanglu game.

Besides, if the Old Madam truly cared for her, she would not have let the housekeeper settle her in the back western courtyard to begin with.

Yet even with her doubts, Shen Weici's expression remained one of grateful tears. She dabbed at the corner of her eye with a handkerchief, her eyes red-rimmed, then stood and addressed the Old Madam: "Weici thanks the Old Madam for her care. But the quarrel between Father and stepmother was Weici's fault. Second Sister was also just acting out of distress — she was not truly bullying me."

"Here before the Old Madam, Weici begs forgiveness on behalf of stepmother and Second Sister."

This performance of self-abasement — taking all the blame on herself — was so complete that even the coldest heart could not remain entirely unmoved.

Lady Wen's face stiffened. Then came the Old Madam's words, seemingly sincere: "What a shame — such a good child, still apologizing after being wronged."

Lady Wen was compelled to stretch a smile, rise, and take Shen Weici's hand, saying: "This was none of your doing at all — it was entirely the servants below who had no sense."

"Consider the matter closed. In future, if anything is withheld or goes missing, come directly to me. Your father is busy and can't keep track of these things — and coming to me will be quicker."

Shen Weici heard the meaning in this perfectly. In future, if anything was needed, she was to go first to her father — and that would make her the unreasonable one.

She kept her face obediently agreeable and nodded.

Coming out of Renshou Hall, Shen Weici felt that the whole scene had been entirely unnecessary. With no one to back her, even if the Old Madam had not intervened, the matter would still have passed this way.

Yuedeng walked beside her and murmured: "I think the Old Madam is quite good to Miss."

Shen Weici pressed her lips together and looked at the plum branches in the distance, just beginning to show buds.

Just then, from behind them came a voice, imperious and carrying: "Shen Weici — stop right there."

Shen Weici paused. She turned to see Shen Zhaozhao bearing down on her with a dark face.

Shen Zhaozhao marched up and narrowed her eyes coldly: "Don't be too pleased with yourself — I'll get it back from you sooner or later."

She gave a cold snort and swept past Shen Weici with her chin in the air.

The gold step-shaker ornaments in her hair swayed and chimed; her embroidered damask fabric radiated wealth; her every manner announced her legitimate daughter's status.

Shen Weici had never wanted any particular quarrel with Shen Zhaozhao — but looking at that imperious attitude, she had nothing to say to her either.

Yuedeng was ready to speak, but Shen Weici gripped her fingers tight, and she swallowed it back once more.

Back at Linchun Courtyard, a young manservant was waiting at the gate. Seeing Shen Weici, he hurried over with a smile and handed her a letter.

Shen Weici could see he had been waiting a while — the cold had him hunching his hands into his sleeves, nearly stamping his feet with the chill. She told Yuedeng to give him a couple extra coins as reward.

She had mentioned to him before that letters from the Zhang household must be placed directly in her own hands. If she was not there, he should come back in a little while. She had not expected the young manservant to actually remember.

Shen Weici went in and sat by the charcoal to read the letter. The last time she had written one to Zhang Yuanheng, Song Zhang had barged in so unexpectedly and said such bewildering things that she had decided the matter between herself and Master Zhang should not be made too conspicuous — and she had not sent it.

He had spoken so sincerely last time, and she had not given him any reply at all. That was not right of her.

The letter was three or four pages long. It opened, as always, with an inquiry about how her character practice was progressing — were there strokes or characters she did not understand, was she getting on with the model texts — and mentioned that once she finished the current volume he would search out more for her.

Two full pages of this. Only in the last two did Zhang Yuanheng say that his grandmother's illness had largely recovered, that his mother would be returning to the capital before long, and that he would then have his mother come to formally propose. He also asked whether the timing felt too hurried.

If it was too soon, he said, after the new year would be just as good.

In the final page, Zhang Yuanheng let a little of his genuine feeling show. He said he was like a young man in the first grip of love — always wanting to be married sooner.

He also wrote that the spring mountains beyond the capital were beautiful in snow, and that he hoped for an opportunity to go and look at it together with her.

And he asked whether she liked the earrings, and told her to tell him honestly.

Shen Weici read through to the last few lines, where Zhang Yuanheng said he could never seem to get a letter back from her, that the first thing he said when he returned home each day was to ask whether a letter had come — always returning empty-handed. He was looking forward to her reply.

Shen Weici's pale eyes softened as they moved across the words. Her fingertips, roasted pink by the charcoal, reached out for the teacup and she took a quiet sip.

Yuedeng loved watching her young mistress read letters. Seeing Shen Weici finish, she eagerly asked: "What did Master Zhang say?"

Her expression was both anxious and expectant — she seemed to care even more than Shen Weici did.

Shen Weici put the letter away and smiled at Yuedeng: "Master Zhang says his mother will be back in the capital before long. She may be coming to propose soon."

Yuedeng's eyes lit with happiness: "Once Miss's marriage is arranged, we can finally leave here!"

Shen Weici smiled and rose to go to the writing desk to reply.

She picked up her brush, dipped it in ink, and looked at the practice volume lying open beside her. She picked it up and examined it carefully.

The practice volume had Zhang Yuanheng's seal in one corner; inside were the marks of places he had annotated. She set the volume down and let the brush fall.

But when she came to actually write, she found she did not know what to say. She was a person of inward emotion, and she simply could not produce the kind of tender, effusive words one might write to Zhang Yuanheng.

She wrote a few characters, set the brush down, picked it up again — and kept at it until late afternoon before she finished.

Yuedeng, seeing Shen Weici struggle so over a single reply, couldn't help smiling: "The first two letters didn't seem to give Miss this much trouble."

Shen Weici sat at the window, propped her cheek on her hand, and gazed outside with a faint smile: "I'm not sure quite why — the Zhang family is coming to propose before long, and suddenly I find myself a little nervous."

Yuedeng pressed a hand to her mouth: "If I were Miss, I'd be nervous too, I think."

After the better part of the afternoon, Shen Weici finally finished. She gave the letter to Yuedeng and told her to take it herself to the front gate, with some money for the errand.

Yuedeng gave an eager sound and went off with the letter.

She was just placing the letter in the hand of Laiku at the front gate when Song Zhang came walking in. For some reason she was a little afraid of him, and instinctively ducked her neck, calling out with the others: "Second Master."

Not until Song Zhang had moved past her did she turn back to Laiku and whisper urgently: "Be careful now — don't lose the letter."

Laiku was one of the Second Lord's men. He knew the situation well and smiled: "Don't worry. Third Young Miss's letters — I won't let anything go wrong."

Yuedeng was satisfied and headed back toward the West Compound.

Song Zhang, past the entrance stone, caught sight of Yuedeng's retreating figure dashing away, and his phoenix eyes moved sideways to Minhe: "That letter should be in my hands within half an hour."

He said it, then paid no more attention to Minhe's fate, and walked on.

Minhe looked at Song Zhang's retreating figure, then tilted his body sideways to look at Laiku, who was heading out the front gate with the letter. He let out a sound under his breath, and followed along behind Laiku.

Who would have thought — their General, going home this early every night and still not enough, and now he had acquired this habit of stealing a look at people's private letters.

Laiku, happily humming along on his errand, had no idea danger was closing in behind him. He walked into an alleyway and suddenly everything went black before his eyes — he let out a shout — and then in an instant it was bright again.

He stood where he was, looking all around him in bewilderment. Not a single person to be seen, not a sound to be heard, only the gusting of a dark wind.

A chill ran through him. Gone was any trace of his earlier leisurely mood. He was frightened enough to break into a run.

chapters.title: Not Worth His Attention
chapters.content:
Song Zhang had the letter in his hands within two quarters of an hour.

The handwriting on it was elegant and small, and carried a faint trace of the soft fragrance that clung to Shen Weici. The seal on the envelope had been pressed closed with wax.

Song Zhang lounged with both long legs propped on the back of a woman kneeling on the floor, opening the letter with unhurried ease.

The woman on the floor was trembling so violently she was nearly flat on the ground, and crying silently without daring to make a sound. She would never volunteer to come to Second Master Song's quarters again.

Minhe stood nearby and watched — kindness and tenderness had never existed in his General's vocabulary. The Princess Consort sent women over every few days, and every last one of them was sent away with her pride in tatters. And yet they still kept coming forward.

Did they really imagine they were the one who would be different?

Only a single page of paper had been folded into the envelope — the characters neat and tidy, carrying a lingering warmth of fragrance. Song Zhang read through to the last line with a flat expression, the letter pinched between his fingers, his dark eyes unreadable.

A long silence — and then came a cold, gritted smile.

So this was her true nature on display. The letter was, word by tender word, full of feeling: she inquired after Zhang Yuanheng's clothing in the cold, urged him not to overwork himself on official business.

She spoke of looking forward to going to the spring mountains together to see the snow. And at the end she had composed lines of poetry — understated in meaning, yet clearly expressive of longing.

She had truly put in the effort.

He supposed this explained why Zhang Yuanheng was so completely taken with her. Words like these, full of warmth and tenderness, issuing from those beautifully enticing lips — what man who read them would not lose his head, would not go out of his way to seek her out?

The letter in his fingers was gripped tighter and tighter. An inexplicable, nameless irritation rose in his chest.

Quite the audacity — and here he had felt sorry for her being cold at night and taken charcoal to her in the middle of the night. And she was nothing but a woman with her sights set on climbing to a better position, with her whole heart bent on ensnaring men.

Well — naturally, given her origins, marriage into an Earldom was an extraordinary stroke of fortune for her.

Last time, had Xu Zhi'an not already been engaged to Shen Zhaozhao, she probably would have set her sights on him too, with the habits she had.

Why was he even giving this woman a second thought?

Song Zhang's expression darkened by degrees. His fingers pressed together and the letter became fragments, startling another tremor out of the woman on the floor.

Song Zhang impatiently kicked the woman out and told her to be gone. His dark eyes churned with some inner turbulence for a few moments — then he rose and walked to Linchun Courtyard.

Inside Linchun Courtyard, Shen Weici was sitting by the charcoal, finishing the last repairs to a garment. She had scraped her finger from needlework a while back and had left it unfinished for some time. With nothing pressing, she thought to finish it quickly.

The outside was still faintly light, but inside the room the candles had been lit, two stands casting a warm brightness through the space. And with two charcoal braziers set inside the room, it was a pleasantly comfortable place to pass the time.

When Song Zhang entered, what he saw was Shen Weici kneeling on the low table to sew, the silken skirt pooled under her knees, her hair only loosely pinned with the silver hairpin, several loose strands hanging down and left unattended. The amber candlelight fell on the fine lines of her face — softness and weariness intertwined, as though carrying the faintest trace of fragrance.

And those half-lowered eyes — the long lashes casting a shadow underneath, translucent in the lamplight; even the tip of her elegant nose held a shimmer of warmth.

What a pity she had such a deplorable character.

In private, exchanging letters with a man — and the letter full of improper things.

Song Zhang looked at her with undisguised contempt. He met Shen Weici's startled upward glance and looked down at her with a cold face, then swept a glance at the charcoal brazier beside her: "Charcoal sent to my courtyard — I hear it ended up here. Is that so?"

Shen Weici was taken aback. The last thing she had expected Song Zhang to say was this. Hearing it was about charcoal, she thought of the charcoal left on the walkway that morning.

She did not understand how charcoal from two completely separate courtyards — one in the east, one in the west, at considerable distance — could possibly be delivered to the wrong place. It was thoroughly bewildering.

But whatever the case, if this charcoal was not hers and its rightful owner had come to her door, it was only proper to return it.

She had a maid bring out two pieces of the charcoal. Looking at them, she could see that the surface was coated in a faint frost — these were indeed different from the ones before.

She looked at Song Zhang: "Is this Young Lord Song's charcoal?"

Song Zhang met her eyes with a cold smile: "Silver-thread charcoal is not something just anyone can use. Aside from me, who else would have it — or dare?"

Shen Weici paused at this. She had heard that silver-thread charcoal was precious — there was no possibility the housekeeper had sent her this. She had also forgotten to check yesterday.

She set down what she was holding and, ignoring Song Zhang's contemptuous gaze directed at her, stood and went to him, offering an apologetic bow in good temper: "The maids didn't know it had been delivered here by mistake. We assumed it was sent by the housekeeper and burned it without thinking. It was our fault — I am sorry."

She had Yuedeng bring what remained, then looked at Song Zhang: "Some was used today. I offer Young Lord Song my apologies, and ask that Young Lord Song not hold it against us."

As she said this, she gave a slight curtsey.

Shen Weici's intention was to treat this with proper courtesy. A few pieces of charcoal — a man like Song Zhang should not care. Yet he had come in person for them, which she could not begin to fathom.

But what came from above was a cold, low snort, followed by Song Zhang's voice, dripping with sarcasm: "Third Young Miss says a few pieces of charcoal and that's the end of it? That is Northern District silver-thread charcoal, specially transported — of considerable value. It is for imperial use. The Emperor gave it as a gift. Is Third Young Miss's apology truly all the reparation she offers?"

Shen Weici had not expected the charcoal to be of imperial use, but the deed was done. She raised her eyes to Song Zhang: "What does Young Lord Song want?"

Song Zhang's gaze passed over Shen Weici from top to bottom, finally resting on her luminous face. His eyes were still cold: "What do you think? Naturally, you repay what was burned."

Shen Weici frowned slightly and looked at Song Zhang: "If Young Lord Song truly says it is imperial use, how am I to obtain it? Burning your charcoal was my wrong — Young Lord Song need only name a sum of silver, and I will repay it."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow: "The Emperor's gift — what price do you put on it?"

"Say the reparation is one hundred taels of silver. Can you even pay it?"

At this, Yuedeng could bear it no longer. She stepped forward: "We didn't know it was Second Master's charcoal. The maids had never seen silver-thread charcoal before — yes, we could see the frosted surface looked different, but we'd never seen anything like it, so naturally we assumed it was what the housekeeper had sent."

"If Second Master wants to call us to account now, it has nothing to do with Miss. Miss wasn't even up when we lit the charcoal. If Second Master must punish someone, punish me — I'm willing to accept it."

Song Zhang looked at the forward little maid who had inserted herself, and his expression went colder: "What a sharp-tongued little maid. I wonder if she'd be this glib after all those teeth were pulled out."

Shen Weici's face went white. She looked at Song Zhang: "Young Lord Song, tell me plainly — what is it you want?"

Song Zhang crossed his arms and looked down at Shen Weici with unmistakable insolence: "Either Third Young Miss thinks carefully about how she intends to repay me — or I will have that maid's teeth pulled out right now."

"Your choice."

Shen Weici looked at Song Zhang, astonished. She voiced the question she had long wanted to ask: "Young Lord Song — why do you treat me this way? What have I done to deserve it?"

Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici's pallid face — the fine, pointed jaw, the full red lips beneath — and raised an eyebrow. He looked at her dark, sweeping brows and clear eyes, cold and light and seemingly amused: "What have you done to deserve it? What do you think you deserve from me?"

Shen Weici lifted her face to look at Song Zhang, her voice a little hoarse: "And what kind of person am I?"

Those entrancing peach-blossom eyes were fixed on him. Her cloud-like hair framed her face, her brows and eyes like a painting — and even this look of apparent innocence could melt a man's heart with startling ease.

Song Zhang looked at Shen Weici's expression and thought of the way she had shyly lowered her head before Zhang Yuanheng, thought of the tender, feeling-laden letter she had written him.

This kind of woman was not worth his attention.

He cursed himself inwardly for going to so much trouble to bring her charcoal.

Beneath Song Zhang's brows lay a cold, scornful light. His dark eyes were heavy with cold, and his low voice held nothing but mockery: "You don't know what kind of person you are?"

He looked at Shen Weici again: "I'll give you a few days to think it over. Once you've decided, come and find me. Otherwise, I can guarantee that maid of yours will not be left with a single tooth."

Song Zhang said this and turned to leave — only to feel a light, soft resistance at his sleeve. He started, turned — and saw that Shen Weici had reached out and taken hold of his sleeve.

And above that was her beautifully enticing face, and those eyes — brimming with the full light of spring water.

chapters.title: Nearly Drew Away His Heart
chapters.content:
The person before him nearly drew Song Zhang's heart from his chest in that instant — yet he hardened himself, feigning indifference, and shook her hand away.

And just as he had barged in without warning, he left in the same careless, sweeping manner.

After Song Zhang left, he thought again of the aggrieved expression on Shen Weici's face, and felt more irritated than before.

His whole mind was full of the feeling-laden letter Shen Weici had written to Zhang Yuanheng.

What a woman with no sense of shame — not even deserving of the charcoal he had brought her.

He kept his face cold, flicked his robe, and strode away.

Inside the room, Shen Weici watched Song Zhang's retreating figure through the window, then sat quietly on the daybed.

Yuedeng came over: "Miss, should we tell the Second Lord? Second Master is truly bullying someone now."

Shen Weici was silent.

When darkness fell, a figure came hurrying into the courtyard and quickly had a maid pass a message inside.

Hearing Laiku had come, Shen Weici paused slightly, then had a maid bring him in.

Laiku came in looking miserable, stood before Shen Weici, and slapped himself on the face: "Third Young Miss — this servant lost the letter."

Shen Weici looked at Laiku and told him not to be frightened — just tell her what had happened.

Hearing Shen Weici's gentle, steady voice, he calmed a little and said in a rush: "Just now this servant was hurrying toward the Earldom with the letter. Everything had been fine up until that point — no one on the road — but when I arrived at the Earldom and reached into my coat, the letter was gone."

"I turned myself inside out looking — nothing. I went back and walked the whole path again — still nothing. To this day I cannot work out where the letter could have disappeared."

Shen Weici heard this and frowned, going back over the contents of the letter in her mind. Fortunately, she had not mentioned her own identity in the letter, nor any reference to the Jian'an Marquis Manor. Even if someone with ill intentions had picked it up, they could not know who had written it.

Furthermore, she had written in the style of the practice volume, to let Zhang Yuanheng offer guidance — a style rarely used by women, making it difficult to guess whose hand it was.

Shen Weici felt somewhat relieved. She looked at Laiku standing there in a panic and said calmly: "I won't hold this against you. But next time be sure to keep it safely on your person — there can be no more mistakes like this."

Laiku nodded rapidly: "Third Young Miss may rest easy — it will never happen again."

He then looked at her carefully: "Could Third Young Miss not mention this to the Second Lord?"

Shen Weici smiled: "Don't worry."

Laiku let out a long breath of relief, beaming, and was about to leave.

Shen Weici stopped him: "If the courtyard runs out of charcoal and there isn't enough — what can be done?"

Laiku paused and said: "Each courtyard's monthly charcoal from the common fund is distributed in set amounts. If you go over, you have to buy it yourself."

He looked at Shen Weici: "Is Third Young Miss short of charcoal?"

Shen Weici smiled without answering, and only asked: "What does charcoal cost outside?"

Laiku thought: "Standard black charcoal is about fifty wen per catty. But that gives off a lot of smoke and fumes."

"Better quality nanmu charcoal is one hundred fifty wen. That's what the Manor uses. And above that, silver-thread charcoal isn't something ordinary people can afford — nearly one tael per catty."

Yuedeng made an involuntary exclamation: "That expensive?"

Laiku laughed: "There are even finer ones above that — the fragrant charcoal for ladies' hand warmers, or the walnut charcoal and olive charcoal used for brewing tea. The varieties are endless."

Shen Weici let Laiku go after that. The thought she had been entertaining of sending him to buy charcoal outside died quietly.

Yuedeng looked at Shen Weici: "Was Miss thinking of buying charcoal?"

Shen Weici said: "This month's courtyard ration has already been used. To go back and ask for more would be improper."

"But to go to Father again — the Second Lady would find out and cause trouble for me. And I've already gone once. Asking again so soon is not right."

"And if we buy charcoal with what's left of our monthly stipend, it won't buy much."

Yuedeng felt the difficulty: "Then how does Miss get through this month?"

"And as for Second Master — if things are hard for Miss, this servant won't let Miss take the fall for me."

Shen Weici pressed a hand to her brow with a sigh: "You spoke up on my behalf — and everything you said was completely right. It is Song Zhang who is being unreasonable."

"You did it for me. I will also look out for you. I won't let him do anything to you. Let's wait a few days and see."

Yuedeng looked at her mistress rubbing her temples with tired fingers, then at the flickering shadows beneath her lowered lashes — vivid pink, the silk-blue robe against skin white as snow, as lovely as a beauty before blossoming flowers.

She stared a moment, and felt, without cause, a kind of grief.

Like the grief of seeing a bright pearl coated in dust.

Her young mistress had never competed with anyone, was always quiet and composed, knew every propriety, and never sought to stand out. So why did one person after another come to torment her?

After more than a month in the Manor, she understood. Great families were all about status and birth. A whole den of wolves and tigers.

Shen Weici looked at the half-repaired garment on the low table — needles and thread scattered, the blue-green fabric catching the light in different hues. That vivid color seemed to mock her.

She could sew no more. Shen Weici rose and went to wash up, then settled into bed early.

In the Manor, even paper was something she had to use sparingly, to say nothing of books for leisure.

Shen Weici thought of the letter that had not been sent, and of Zhang Yuanheng's eager letters and his certain expectation of a reply. She did not want Zhang Yuanheng's enthusiasm to cool. Already out of her outer garments and in bed, she put them back on and got up, intending to write a second letter so Laiku could take it in the morning.

Yuedeng came in carrying the warming brick and immediately tried to stop her: "It's so cold — what is Miss getting up for? The charcoal from before is nearly spent too. Your chill had just barely cleared — if you catch another one, there's no silver left for medicine."

Shen Weici stopped. She naturally had no desire to fall ill again, and obediently lay back down.

She leaned against the soft pillow at her back and watched Yuedeng put the warming brick into her covers, while Yuedeng chattered on: "This Manor looks as though you'd never need to spend money on anything — but the moment you want to get anything done, everything costs silver."

"Even telling a servant to do a simple errand — you have to give a tip or they won't move. I don't know where that rule came from."

Shen Weici listened to her chatter. The warming brick had warmed her through, and she curled deeper under the covers.

Yuedeng then brought medicine to apply to the scratch on her jaw and gave a soft exclamation — she leaned in close to look, and said quietly: "Miss — this wound looks like it's almost healed already. It's scabbing over."

Yuedeng gently lifted the scab with her fingernail; it came away in a fleck of dark red, leaving a faint pink line.

Yuedeng quickly reapplied a layer of medicine: "The medicine the Second Lord gave really does work. Though looking at it, there isn't much left. I'm not sure how many more applications it can manage."

She said it, then immediately took it back: "No, no — best if we never need it again."

She looked at Shen Weici: "Does Miss want another warming brick?"

Shen Weici shook her head, and told Yuedeng to go to sleep as well.

chapters.title: The Banquet at the Zhang Household
chapters.content:
On the day of the banquet, Lady Wen specially sent someone to tell Shen Weici to dress with care — and even dispatched a matron to come and style her hair.

On ordinary days, Shen Weici wore simple hairstyles. Yuedeng did not know the capital's fashionable women's styles, and before Shen Weici came of age her hair had been worn half-up; now that she was of age and the hair should be pinned properly, the more elaborate styles were beyond Yuedeng, and Shen Weici had never minded, so nothing had been changed.

The matron Lady Wen had sent was swift and skilled. Standing behind Shen Weici and holding the flowing cascade of black hair, she said admiringly: "Third Young Miss has such soft, dark hair — smooth as silk. Once it's properly pinned, it will look beautiful."

Shen Weici herself had little investment in her hair, but she suddenly remembered the last time Lady Wen had sent the seamstress to make her clothing. She quietly called Yuedeng to stand nearby and watch — in case the matron tried something similar with her hair.

Yuedeng caught Shen Weici's meaning, stood to the side claiming she wanted to learn, and watched without blinking.

Fortunately the matron seemed genuinely focused on her work. With practiced hands, in no time at all she had styled Shen Weici's hair into a rather elaborate crossed-knot coif.

She then asked Shen Weici to bring out her ornaments. Shen Weici had Yuedeng fetch the box Shen Zhaozhao had sent. The matron looked at it and saw they were all somewhat outdated in the capital's fashion, but there was enough to work with.

She selected two jade hairpins and fastened them in, then bent to clip the jadeite earrings at Shen Weici's ears. She looked at the figure in the mirror — eyes dark as lacquer, lips red as cinnabar, a delicate oval face both fragile and lovely, with those peach-blossom eyes and the beauty-mark mole, like a spray of flowers heavy with dew.

In the way she held herself there was the poise of swaying autumn air, and in looks and bearing she was, if anything, a shade above Second Young Miss.

She kept this impression to herself, however, and straightened up, asking: "Does Third Young Miss have any pearl powder?"

Shen Weici shook her head: "I've never used it."

Matron Tan looked at her face — as white and smooth as fine mutton-fat jade. It made no difference either way.

She added: "The carriages are ready at the front gate. We leave at the hour of si. It must be nearly time — Third Young Miss should finish getting ready and make her way to the front gate."

With that, she had nothing more to say and left.

The moment the matron was gone, Yuedeng leaned close and gazed at Shen Weici with admiration: "Miss looks so beautiful dressed up."

But Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng with a faint furrow of concern: "By rights, at this kind of occasion, whether or not the Second Lady brings me along shouldn't matter much — given how little she cares for me, she really should not have bothered."

"And yet she sent a matron all the way to style my hair. That wasn't truly necessary. My ordinary appearance would have drawn no one's attention at a gathering like this."

"Besides, she clearly doesn't want me outshining Shen Zhaozhao. Usually she's glad for me to keep to myself — and yet this time she seems to be putting me on display."

Yuedeng went to fetch the white-ground cloud-and-water printed cloak and stood before Shen Weici to help her put it on: "Last time didn't the Second Lady say she wanted Miss to look respectable? I imagine it's for the sake of the Manor's reputation."

Shen Weici lowered her eyes as Yuedeng tied the cord at her throat. A breath of wind came in from outside, and she sighed: "I'm not so sure."

But she said no more about it. Once Shen Weici was ready, she set out with Yuedeng.

On this rare occasion of making a real effort with her appearance, the result was striking — a blue-ground pink-flower cloud-brocade skirt, with pink winding-branch patterns, her figure graceful and elegant. The smoke-blue earrings swayed against her face, and her skin in the daylight was startlingly white.

The maids of Linchun Courtyard all stared, and each one eagerly wanted to come along and see the world. But Shen Weici feared that too many maids might cause accidents; and besides, her maids had mostly been rough-work girls before, unfamiliar with outside propriety. If they blundered into some restriction or taboo, she would be hard pressed to manage the consequences.

So she said, gently but firmly, that they could come another time.

The maids were compliant and did not press.

At the front gate, a servant greeted Shen Weici with a smile: "Third Young Miss, this way please."

She followed and saw three carriages waiting at the gate, grandly appointed. The manservant up front reported: "Third Lady and First Master and Fourth Master are already in their carriage — Second Lady and Third Young Miss have not come yet."

Shen Weici asked casually: "What about Fourth Young Miss and Fifth Young Miss?"

The manservant paused at one of the carriages and held back the curtain, smiling: "Fourth Young Miss and Fifth Young Miss are not going."

Shen Weici heard this, gave a small nod, and bent to climb in.

When Yuedeng tried to follow, the manservant directed her to the rear carriage.

Inside the carriage it was quite spacious. Shen Weici sat and lifted a corner of the curtain to look outside. The carriage ahead was presumably the Second Branch's. The First Branch's Princess Consort Huimin was, as expected, absent again.

After a while, Lady Wen appeared with Shen Zhaozhao. Shen Weici let the curtain fall.

Lady Wen and Shen Zhaozhao boarded and the three of them sat together. Shen Weici spoke first, in a quiet voice: "Second Lady. Second Sister."

Lady Wen glanced at Shen Weici. The carriage light was dim; she looked cursorily — and then lifted the curtain to get a better look. Shen Weici sat with perfect composure by the window-side, hands resting on her knees with a handkerchief between her fingers, the lower halves of her fingers bare; her earrings brushed her white jade cheek, and as she gave a slight bow of the head and then raised her eyes again, it was a sight that startled Lady Wen.

She let the curtain fall. She gave a cool sound of acknowledgement and said no more.

Shen Weici also stayed quiet. She felt a gaze on her and knew it was Shen Zhaozhao from across the carriage, but did not raise her head.

Outside, the quiet gradually gave way to the lively sounds of street vendors calling their wares. Shen Weici had not been out of the Manor since arriving in the capital more than a month ago, and she was suddenly curious. Her fingers had just started to move toward the curtain when Lady Wen's cool, low voice came from across the carriage: "What — do you think so highly of yourself that you want the people outside to see you too?"

Shen Weici's hand stilled at these words. She withdrew her fingers.

At the Zhang household gate, firecrackers could already be heard from a distance; drawing closer, the sounds intensified, and there was a constant noise of voices. They had not yet descended from the carriage and already one could tell the occasion was lively beyond compare.

Maids came down from the rear carriages; a matron lifted the curtain to help those in the main carriage descend.

Shen Weici was last out. Stepping down, she could see numerous carriages drawn up before the Zhang household's great gate, with dedicated manservants guiding each one to its place.

Lady Wen ran into an acquaintance at the entrance and pulled the Third Lady-in-law Wang aside to chat. Shen Weici quietly followed at the rear.

She knew no one here and was afraid of causing some mistake.

A greeter came forward to lead Lady Wen and her party inside, but at that moment two eunuchs came running forward, shouting: "The Noble Consort arrives — make way!"

Everyone at the entrance froze and looked to one side. Two rows of armored guards escorted two exceptionally magnificent carriages forward, and people on either side stepped back of their own accord.

Shen Weici also looked over, and saw the procession was vast: ten eunuchs walking in front, some ten palace maids flanking the sides, and at the very head, mounted on horseback, was the Imperial Feathered Guard Commander Song Zhang.

Song Zhang wore a great red robe embroidered with coiling serpents, one hand holding the reins, the other a riding crop; two black-and-gold swords hung at his waist. His expression was haughty and languid, contemptuous of all below him.

Zhang Tingyi came hurrying forward from the crowd of guests, and following the eunuchs' announcement, knelt with everyone else: "We welcome the Noble Consort—"

chapters.title: Seeing Zhang Tingyi at the Banquet
chapters.content:
The gates of the Zhang household were thronged like a marketplace. Every person of rank and influence in the capital had come to pay court.

All the more so when Noble Consort Zhang arrived in person today — demonstrating the depth of the Emperor's favor. Those seeking to curry favor would be even more numerous.

A woman of the inner palace was normally not permitted to leave even when a family member died. Yet Noble Consort Zhang's mother was turning seventy, and the Emperor had granted her leave to attend the celebration — and moreover dispatched the Commander of the Imperial Feathered Guard himself to ride ahead and clear the path. This alone said everything about how favored Noble Consort Zhang was within the palace.

The Imperial Feathered Guard was charged with protecting the imperial family's movements, but having the Guard Commander personally escort someone was reserved only for the Emperor himself. Today's display had made it plain: the Emperor was giving the Zhang household every honor, and Zhang Tingyi's position at court was at its zenith.

The imperial carriage halted before the Zhang household gate. Song Zhang reined in his horse and looked around the assembly. His gaze passed over Shen Weici, who had knelt with the crowd — just a glance — and then he dismounted and went to Noble Consort Zhang's carriage, lifting the curtain for her.

The eunuch in front cried: "The Noble Consort descends — do not look directly upon her."

Everyone bowed their heads lower.

Noble Consort Zhang placed her hand in Song Zhang's and stepped down. She walked to the front, where her elder brother Zhang Tingyi stood: "Brother — take me to see Mother."

Zhang Tingyi hurried to fall in beside his sister and escort her inside.

Fifth Princess Zhao Rou, who had been following behind Noble Consort Zhang, looked back when she saw Song Zhang not following the group but walking the other way. She reached back and tugged his sleeve: "Why aren't you coming inside?"

Song Zhang glanced at the Fifth Princess and said with restrained patience, clasping his hands: "Your subject still needs to arrange the guards for Noble Consort's safety. I shall withdraw for now."

He did not wait for Zhao Rou to speak again, turned, and walked back toward the attendant guards.

Zhao Rou pouted at Song Zhang's retreating figure, stamped her foot in annoyance, then heard her mother calling for her ahead and quickly followed.

Once the Noble Consort had entered, the rest of the assembly finally rose from the ground.

Shen Weici stood among the crowd. She looked to one side — and saw Song Zhang standing before some twenty or so palace guards, his brows arched in arrogance, his red robe snapping in the wind as he issued what appeared to be instructions.

She looked away and then saw Lady Wen and Third Lady-in-law Wang heading into the residence. She hurried to catch up.

Behind her, Song Zhang seemed to sense something. He turned his head slightly — and caught just a glimpse of a trailing edge of smoky pink as it disappeared through the gate.

Shen Weici's party, once inside, was led by servants toward the rear garden. Only then did she understand that the Zhang household's grounds were a world unto themselves — fine trees clustered thickly, rare flowers blazed with color. On both sides rose soaring buildings cutting into the sky, with intricately carved ridgelines and embroidered balustrades, and everywhere stone steps wound up through clouds with white stone balustrades — all speaking of extraordinary wealth. Compared to the Jian'an Marquis Manor, this looked even grander.

The wives and female guests were led to the rear garden. Old Madam Zhang was seated in the main rear hall. Lady Wen, with no title or honorific to her name, was not eligible to sit in the same room as the Noble Consort. She could only go before Old Madam Zhang, say a few words of felicitation, show herself, and then withdraw.

Shen Weici followed behind Lady Wen and went inside. Looking up, she saw Noble Consort Zhang seated beside Old Madam Zhang at the head — and to either side were first-rank Duchesses, County Mistresses, imperially enfeoffed ladies, and the like.

Even though they were of the Jian'an Marquis household, in this hall they still had to kneel in ceremonial greeting before the Noble Consort. Only when the eunuch beside her announced they could rise were they permitted to stand and approach Old Madam Zhang to offer birthday congratulations.

After the full ceremony, Lady Wen nudged Shen Weici forward with a smile, asking her to wish the Old Madam long life before everyone.

Shen Weici noticed that even Shen Zhaozhao had not come forward and was still standing behind her mother, yet Lady Wen was pushing her to the front. She had little choice but to step up and offer a few phrases of good fortune and long life in a clear, warm voice.

She thought it would end there, and was about to step back — when Noble Consort Zhang spoke from the side: "Such a graceful and lovely young lady — and her voice is pleasant to listen to as well."

She smiled toward Lady Wen: "Second Lady Shen, you are fortunate."

Noble Consort Zhang was not unfamiliar with the Jian'an Marquis household. Before she had left home, the great families' daughters had all known one another, and besides, Princess Consort Huimin had married into the household, and Song Zhang was trusted by the Emperor. Her own daughter, the Fifth Princess, was the Emperor's choice for Song Zhang's betrothal. So she knew the household better than most.

Lady Wen, delighted by the Noble Consort's praise of Shen Weici, quickly agreed: "This is the Manor's Third Young Miss — only recently brought back to us. I am her stepmother and am raising her as my own. She is indeed a pleasing child."

Noble Consort Zhang, hearing Lady Wen's words, studied Shen Weici once more with narrow, appraising eyes. She had recently been thinking of selecting a gentle and composed side consort for the Fourth Prince, and the young woman before her was attractive enough in both face and bearing, and she was of the Jian'an Marquis household. If she had been the legitimate daughter it would have been better still — but she was concubine-born, which was a pity.

She withdrew her gaze and exchanged a few more courteous words with Lady Wen, then Lady Wen took Shen Weici and Shen Zhaozhao and withdrew.

Outside, matrons led them toward seating in the rear garden.

The rear garden was already full of guests. Across pavilions and terraces, richly dressed ladies and young misses stood in clusters of two, three, and four, talking and laughing. The air was thick with the scent of face powder.

Only now did Shen Weici truly understand that the capital was indeed full of high-ranking families at every turn. Lady Wen, who had been born into an aristocratic family, could only be counted as ordinary here.

Lady Wen went off to find an old friend, reminded Shen Zhaozhao not to wander too far so she could be found when the banquet started, and finally said to Shen Weici: "You're not familiar with anyone — just stay with Zhaozhao."

Shen Weici watched Lady Wen's retreating figure toward the pavilion, then saw Shen Zhaozhao waving to an acquaintance she recognized, clearly with no intention of looking after her. She took the hint and did not follow, but went to sit in a nearby pavilion.

The position was visible, not far from Lady Wen's pavilion, so Shen Weici could follow along easily if something came up.

And the pavilion had only two other young ladies already chatting inside, which was quiet enough.

She sat to one side, leaning against the railing, letting the cool breeze wash over her, looking out at the lake — its green surface rippling in soft waves.

Yuedeng whispered in awe beside her: "The Zhang household is really something. Look at this lake — you could actually go boating on it."

Just as she spoke, an excited voice nearby exclaimed: "Is that the Fourth Prince and General Song on the far bank?"

Shen Weici startled, and felt several women near her move to look across the water. She glanced in the same direction.

The two banks of the lake were not far apart. The women were all on this side; the men were across the water.

Shen Weici raised her eyes slightly and saw two figures standing at a balcony railing on the far bank — one in red, one in dark. Both were looking toward the lake, apparently in conversation.

Shen Weici could not make out their faces from across the water, but she guessed immediately that the figure in red was Song Zhang.

Then someone nearby murmured: "I hear General Song has no wife yet — because of an injury he suffered in the army. Lots of people have been saying so."

Another voice quickly cut in: "Be careful what you say. I've heard His Majesty intends to betroth the Fifth Princess to General Song. If that's true, would His Majesty arrange such a marriage?"

Shen Weici had heard enough by this point and let her gaze drift away from the far bank.

chapters.title: Encountering Song Zhang at the Zhang Estate
chapters.content:
After sitting for a while longer, Shen Weici noticed a maidservant standing beside the garden pavilion. She sent Yuedeng over to ask how much longer before the banquet would begin. Yuedeng returned to report that it would be nearly another hour before it started.

Shen Weici was unfamiliar with the estate and could not wander too far, so she remained in her spot, surrounded by faces she did not recognize.

As she let her gaze drift idly across the lake once more, she caught sight of a familiar figure on the opposite bank. The man stood among a small group, yet she had the distinct feeling that his eyes kept drifting back to her.

Because they were standing on a waterside pavilion that jutted out over the lake, they were not too far apart, and Shen Weici could clearly make out that the person across the water was Zhang Yuanheng.

She paused for a moment, then saw that Zhang Yuanheng was also looking at her — smiling at her from within the crowd, his bright eyes shining. In the midst of this unfamiliar, unsettling environment, that smile brought her a measure of calm. Thinking that she now had someone steady and dependable by her side, she could not help but let a smile touch her own eyes in return.

Zhang Yuanheng was momentarily stunned by that smile. He noticed, too, that Shen Weici was dressed more elaborately today than her usual understated style, which made her look even more striking. The jade hairpin nestled in her dark hair and the earrings swaying beside her face were simply breathtaking.

Someone called his name twice and received no response. That person followed Zhang Yuanheng's gaze and asked with a laugh: "Who is Brother Zhang looking at? You've gone completely dazed."

"Is that some beauty over there? Should I call out to her, so she knows of Brother Zhang's feelings?"

Only then did Zhang Yuanheng come back to his senses, and he turned to his companions with a sheepish bow. "Gentlemen, please don't tease me."

But then he saw his friend craning his neck to peer across the water and quickly moved to block his line of sight. "What's so worth looking at? Surely talking with me is more important than ogling beauties?"

For his trouble, he got a punch in the chest. "You were the one not paying attention."

Shen Weici watched Zhang Yuanheng and his companions banter with a suppressed smile. When she turned her head, however, her eyes swept over something and her expression stiffened.

On the covered walkway across the way, Song Zhang stood talking with a group of people. For no clear reason she could name, she had the distinct sense that he was watching her with those cold, icy eyes of his.

She had done nothing, and yet she felt as though she had been caught doing something shameful.

After sitting for a while longer, the covered walkway across the way was empty of people. When she turned again, she saw the women nearby rise and look toward the front. Following their gaze, she spotted the Imperial Consort leading the Fifth Princess, along with several noblewomen who were close to her, heading off to stroll through the Chaolu Garden.

A great procession of eunuchs and maidservants swept around them like a dark, pressing crowd. Wherever they passed, everyone stepped aside.

Then she noticed a dainty, richly dressed young woman reaching out repeatedly to tug at Song Zhang's sleeve as he walked alongside the procession. The girl tilted her head up as if speaking to him and even reached out her fingers to touch the sword at his waist.

That must be the Fifth Princess the others had just been whispering about.

Song Zhang's expression was unreadable — probably still that unpredictable shift between displeasure and indifference — yet he appeared to be tolerating the Fifth Princess's indiscriminate pawing at him.

Someone nearby murmured quietly: "They say the Fifth Princess is willful and spoiled, but looking at her beside General Song, she doesn't seem quite like the rumors say."

Another replied in an undertone: "Rumors don't rise from nothing. Perhaps she's only like this in front of General Song."

Shen Weici watched in silence as the procession moved past. When she turned again, she happened to catch a glimpse of Madam Wen heading toward the rear main courtyard with a maidservant, while Shen Zhaohao was nowhere to be seen nearby. After a short while, she saw Wencui — Madam Wen's head maidservant — standing in the open, scanning the area as if searching for someone. At last Wencui's eyes met Shen Weici's, and she came hurrying over.

Shen Weici looked on and stood up, bringing Yuedeng along. She watched Wencui stride toward her and say: "Third Miss, please don't wander off. Come with me — the Madam may be asking for you shortly."

With that, Wencui led Shen Weici toward the hall where they had paid their respects to Old Madam Zhang.

The courtyard ahead was wide and open. Shen Weici asked: "Is Second Elder Sister not coming?"

Wencui glanced at Shen Weici and smiled slightly. "The Second Miss is probably deep in lively conversation with the other young ladies right now. The Madam said to let the Second Miss be."

As they were speaking, a maidservant named Xiaohong came out from inside and greeted Shen Weici with a smile: "Third Miss, the Madam is asking you to come in and sit with her."

At these words, Shen Weici felt something was not quite right.

How was it that Madam Wen was keeping her by her side? Wouldn't Shen Zhaohao be a more fitting choice?

Shen Weici was about to ask, but Xiaohong urged her with a smile: "The Madam is still waiting, Third Miss — please hurry."

Shen Weici had no choice but to follow Xiaohong inside.

The place, which had been lively just a short while ago, was now somewhat quieter.

While sitting in the pavilion earlier, she had overheard a fair bit of gossip — that Zhang Tingyi had married twice and kept countless women beside him, yet had only one son, and that son was simple-minded. Someone had even whispered that the foolish boy might not be his.

Now that the Imperial Consort Zhang had left, the only people remaining by Old Madam Zhang's side were longtime friends of hers, a few fawning noblewomen, and some distant relatives.

Shen Weici looked at Madam Wen's brilliantly smiling face. She had never seen the woman smile so ingratiatingly before. This, she concluded, must be a case of flattery in action.

Bearing the weight of glances from all sides, she walked quietly over to Madam Wen's side. When Madam Wen saw her, she smiled and said: "Come sit beside me. You're not familiar with anyone here, so it's better you stay close."

Shen Weici looked at Madam Wen's warm, smiling face, pressed her lips together, and sat down beside her.

A woman nearby smiled at Madam Wen: "How kind-hearted you are — even this generous toward a concubine-born daughter."

Madam Wen replied: "Her mother is gone, so I raise her as my own. What does birth status matter?"

The noblewomen present all burst into praise for Madam Wen's magnanimity.

Shen Weici listened in silence, her face betraying no expression whatsoever.

After a while, someone entered from outside.

The newcomer was dressed in a purple everyday robe, appeared to be around fifty years of age, and carried himself with an alert, upright, capable bearing. His ornamentation was lavish — a golden crown, a jade-studded belt, and three or four jade thumb rings on his fingers. Several attendants followed behind him.

He walked directly to Old Madam Zhang, who sat at the head of the room, and paid his respects, then went forward to ask whether anything had been overlooked in the arrangements.

Old Madam Zhang smiled: "Don't trouble yourself with this — go back out and tend to the guests. Just rein in that temper of yours and drink a little less."

Zhang Tingyi smiled, then lingered a moment longer beside his mother before preparing to leave. Suddenly, Madam Wen stood up and pulled Shen Weici forward with her: "Weici, come quickly and pay your respects to Master Zhang."

Shen Weici was tugged to her feet by Madam Wen. Her gaze fell on the cluster of embroidered flowers at the center of Zhang Tingyi's chest, and she had no choice but to steel herself and speak: "Greetings, Master Zhang."

Zhang Tingyi heard a soft, melodious voice and startled, looking down to find the source. He saw gently downcast brows and eyes, and earrings that shimmered against a fair complexion — the slant of those eye corners carried the grace of a lotus. She was radiant beyond description.

Zhang Tingyi stared, momentarily entranced. He had always been a man who coveted beauty, and his mind stirred at once. He turned to Madam Wen and asked: "Is this a young lady from the Marquis's household?"
